study_design_identified: Cross-sectional spatial household survey (probabilistic 500 m grid sampling of 120 households integrated with GIS thematic mapping and descriptive statistics)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The primary empirical design is a single-wave quantitative cross-sectional survey of 120 households sampled on a 500 m spatial grid in Mbour to examine spatial and descriptive associations between poverty and water access/affordability, without a longitudinal cohort or quasi-experimental intervention comparator (ruling out ROBINS-I and JBI Cohort). Although Section 2.1 briefly notes in one sentence that interviews were conducted with officials from four water/municipal agencies, no qualitative methodology, coding, thematic analysis, or mixed-methods integration is presented, ruling out MMAT and CASP per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
overall_rating: High concern
selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: While a systematic 500 m spatial grid covering Mbour (120 grid cells, excluding the municipal soccer stadium) was used with a reported 99.19% response rate (Sections 2-2.1, PDF pp. 2-3), selecting only one household per 25-hectare cell near the GPS centroid without documented household/respondent eligibility rules or population-density weighting under-samples high-density poor districts relative to low-density tourist zones and introduces spatial representation bias when extending one household's attributes to the entire mesh cell.
measurement_bias: High concern: Household economic status relies on undocumented questionnaire items that conflate consumption and income and apply an ad hoc 600 CFA franc poverty line (Sections 2.2 and 3.2, PDF pp. 3, 5). Daily per-capita water availability (Water Access Index) uses differential measurement modes (bi-monthly utility bills for paying households versus estimated container and tank capacities for non-paying households; Section 3.4, PDF p. 6) and benchmarks domestic water use against national total per-capita water withdrawals (0.58 m3/person/day, or 580 L/person/day). Claims of polluted well water (PDF pp. 1, 7) are unsupported by microbiological or chemical water testing.
confounding: High concern: No statistical adjustment, stratification, or multivariable regression is conducted to account for confounders of the water-poverty relationship (such as municipal SDE pipe network reach at expanding urban boundaries, informal/unparceled land tenure, household size, or tourism-driven neighborhood heterogeneity). Inferences rely solely on visual comparison of univariate GIS maps.
attrition: Low concern / Not applicable (cross-sectional design): There is no longitudinal follow-up, and household survey non-response is reported as very low (99.19% response rate across 120 households in Section 2.1, PDF p. 3, though 119/120 equals 99.17% and exact refusal/replacement counts are not reported).
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: No survey instrument or pre-analysis protocol is provided. Although Section 2 and Section 2.1 (PDF pp. 2-3) state that indicators of water quality and sanitation were established, that interviews were conducted with four institutional agencies, and that SPSS statistical processing and geostatistical autocorrelation/interpolation models were used, no sanitation data, water-quality measurements, interview analyses, correlation coefficients, confidence intervals, or spatial autocorrelation parameters are reported in Results; several key percentages are drawn from an unpublished Master's thesis (Toure, 2009).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Legal, regulatory, and tariff frameworks—specifically the 1995 Senegalese water sector reform (cited in the Abstract, PDF p. 1), urban encroachment of Mbour onto the rural community of Malicounda (Section 3.1, PDF p. 4), unparceled squatter settlements (Section 2, PDF p. 3), and the disparity between standpipe prices (1750 CFA francs/m3) and the SDE social tariff (191 CFA francs/m3; Section 4, PDF p. 7)—are referenced only as contextual narrative assertions without primary statutory/contractual citations or household/spatial coding of legal exposure.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Water access and water-poverty outcomes suffer from unvalidated survey instruments, differential measurement across billed and unbilled households, lack of physical inspection or water-quality testing, extrapolation of a single centroid household's response to an entire 500 m x 500 m (25-hectare) urban grid cell (Section 2, PDF p. 3), and miscalibrated Water Access Index cutoffs (0-0.25 m3/person/day labeled 'very low access' by misapplying national agricultural/industrial/municipal water withdrawal averages to household domestic consumption; Section 3.4, PDF p. 6).
where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 1 Introduction (PDF pp. 1-2); Section 2 Materials and methods, Section 2.1 Data processing, and Section 2.2 Calculation of the poverty rate (PDF pp. 2-3); Section 3 Results and discussion, Subsections 3.1-3.4 and Figs. 6-11 (PDF pp. 4-6); Section 4 Conclusions and Acknowledgments (PDF pp. 6-7).

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative key-informant interview study (19 semi-structured interviews across 5 purposively selected country cases, informed by literature review and secondary qualitative data synthesis)
why_tool_chosen: S535 collects and thematically analyzes primary qualitative semi-structured interviews with 19 senior leaders in national and local regulators (informed by a narrative literature synthesis and qualitative secondary data coding), with no quantitative empirical component or systematic review synthesis; therefore, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching appraisal tool under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 Can't tell item: Q8 data analysis rigor; 0 No items)
selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern for broader transferability: purposive 'positive outliers within positive outliers' sampling targeted 19 senior leaders in 5 reform-leading countries (with snowball referrals, zero local regulator interviews in Mozambique, no reported non-response rate and no inclusion of informal pit emptiers, households or municipal health/environment regulators).
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: findings rely on self-reported accounts from senior regulatory managers interviewed remotely in English, with explicit risk of social desirability bias (informants had often gained international recognition for sector reform) and no independent field observation or triangulation with informal sanitation workers or municipal enforcement officers.
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative thematic study with no quantitative causal effect estimation; donor/IFI financing and national institutional differences are discussed narratively as contextual influences).
attrition: Not applicable to single-timepoint qualitative interviews (note: initial invitation refusal count is unreported, and >70% of the 19 interviewees responded to manuscript validation member-checking).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: Section 2.6 states that only consensus themes raised consistently across multiple locations were included in Results (potentially under-reporting divergent or negative cases), and illustrative quotes lack anonymized participant codes (e.g., P1–P19) to verify spread across informants, partially mitigated by open deposition of anonymized transcripts in the Cranfield CERES repository.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate for qualitative institutional inquiry: Table 3 maps national regulatory structures, constitutional backing, service standards, and legal status of manual pit emptying across Kenya, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia citing primary regulatory ordinances/guidelines [59–63], supplemented by qualitative accounts of conflicting local municipal bylaws and de facto amnesties, though local bylaws are not doctrinally catalogued.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / not directly measured: sanitation service scaling, safe emptying practices and voluntary compliance are captured solely through senior regulators' qualitative perceptions rather than empirical measurements of safe faecal sludge containment, transport, disposal or public health outcomes.
where_found: Methods and ethics: PDF Pages 3–7 (Sections 2.1–2.6, Tables 1–2); Legal/institutional mapping and qualitative results: PDF Pages 7–10 (Sections 3.1–3.5, Table 3); Discussion, reflexivity and limitations: PDF Pages 10–13 (Sections 4.1–4.4); Data availability and author contributions: PDF Pages 2 and 14.

study_design_identified: Primary mixed-methods study combining an analytical cross-sectional stratified random household survey (N = 396) analyzed via linear and logistic multiple regression with purposively sampled semi-structured in-depth interviews (n = 18)
why_tool_chosen: The Methods section explicitly specifies and executes a primary mixed-methods empirical design pairing a quantitative household survey (N = 396) for Aim 1 with qualitative in-depth interviews (n = 18) for Aim 2, integrating both strands across financial, physical, and social resource domains. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT is the single matching appraisal instrument, applying Qualitative items 1.1–1.5, Quantitative non-randomized items 3.1–3.5 (matching the analytical cross-sectional multivariable regression component), and Mixed-Methods integration items 5.1–5.5.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (14 Yes, 2 No [3.2, 5.5], 1 Can't tell [3.5]; no numeric score per MMAT 2018 guidance, with overall quality bounded by self-report/exposure misclassification and cross-sectional limitations in the quantitative component)
selection_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: Within the study neighborhood (Pinget), selection bias for the quantitative component was very low, using an updated neighborhood census sampling frame (1,793 housing units), stratified random sampling by subdistrict (purok) and tenancy status, and a 95.2% response rate (N = 396). However, Pinget was purposively selected as a single neighborhood within Baguio City, and the qualitative interview subsample (n = 18) was purposively sampled from survey respondents with intentional oversampling of women (15 women, 3 men), limiting external generalizability beyond Pinget.
measurement_bias: High / some concern: All exposures and outcomes relied on respondent self-report and recall during a single dry season that was wetter than usual. Notably, the author documents systematic misclassification in the hypothetical social borrowing network exposure (water-secure households that had never needed to borrow reported zero network size), recall bias in estimated dry-season water consumption, and reliance on unvalidated subjective 11-point scales for cleanliness and ease without objective water-quality or meter verification.
confounding: Moderate concern: Multiple linear and logistic regressions controlled for respondent gender, education, marital status, age, ethnicity, household size, homeownership, and concurrent financial, physical, and social resources, while accounting for compound clustering and finite population correction. However, the cross-sectional design precludes temporal precedence (reverse causality/simultaneity between water expenditures, storage investments, and consumption), and spatial/institutional confounders such as terrain elevation/water pressure, distance to BWD mains, and formal legal land title versus informal settlement status were not directly measured.
attrition: Low concern: The stratified random household survey achieved a 95.2% participation rate among eligible housing units (396/416), and item-level missingness was low (0% to 6.6% for most variables; 12.4% for income) and rigorously handled using multiple imputation with fully conditional specification across 10 imputed datasets incorporating auxiliary variables.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell on pre-registration: No pre-registered study protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported, and two outcomes (perceived ease and affordability) as well as social network exposures were categorized/dichotomized post hoc based on observed data distributions and skewness. Mitigating this concern, the author reports that robustness checks using alternate functional forms of dependent variables and covariate subsets produced consistent results, and null or unexpected regression findings (for savings, homeownership, and borrowing networks) are transparently reported.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / weak-to-adequate concern: Institutional access to the federally authorized municipal utility (Baguio Water District, BWD) was operationalized via self-reported connection tiers (none, shared/some other way, own household metered connection) alongside self-reported homeownership and permanent/boarding tenancy stratification, and qualitatively contextualized with connection fee rules (₱6,000 fee plus ₱4,000–₱8,000 piping costs, case-by-case installment plans, and informal 'under the table' processing barriers). However, formal legal land tenure, municipal eligibility ordinances, and official BWD billing/meter records were not independently verified.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak concern: Water security was operationalized across four distinct dimensions—reported consumption (liters per capita per day), perceived cleanliness (PCA score of five 11-point items for non-drinking domestic uses), perceived ease (11-point scale dichotomized at 8–10), and affordability (monthly water expenses as percentage of income dichotomized at <=10%)—with enumerator assistance to estimate container volumes. However, measures were unvalidated, relied on recall during an atypically wet dry season, excluded drinking-water safety from the cleanliness scale, and lacked physical or microbiological verification.
where_found: Study aims on PDF Pages 3 and 7 (pp. 490, 494); institutional setting (Baguio Water District and Pinget) on PDF Pages 6-7 (pp. 493-494); quantitative survey sampling, variable measurement, multiple imputation, and regression methods on PDF Pages 7-10 (pp. 494-497); qualitative sampling and NVivo coding on PDF Page 10 (p. 497); quantitative results and resource-specific limitations on PDF Pages 10-16 (pp. 497-503); qualitative findings and mixed-methods integration on PDF Pages 17-20 (pp. 504-507); study strengths and limitations on PDF Page 20 (p. 507).

study_design_identified: Quasi-experimental comparative policy evaluation using kernel propensity score matching (PSM) combined with first-differences panel estimation across municipal census waves (with auxiliary cross-sectional survey comparisons)
why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I is the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because the study is a non-randomized comparative evaluation of a formal legal/institutional governance intervention (municipal adoption of usos y costumbres following Oaxaca's 1995 constitutional reform versus a political-party governance comparator arm) estimated via propensity score matching (PSM) and first-differences across census waves. MMAT was not selected because the paper's explicit 'multi-method approach' ([PDF Page 4]) refers to combining PSM with first-differences rather than a qualitative-quantitative mixed-methods design; brief background references to field observations in Section 3 lack any qualitative sampling, data collection, or analysis protocol.
overall_rating: Serious
selection_bias: Moderate risk: The primary analysis covers nearly the entire municipal universe of Oaxaca (564 of 570 municipalities within common support; 418 treated, 146 controls), minimizing sample exclusion bias, but treatment assignment is self-selected by communities in 1995, treatment status is fixed retroactively at the year-2000 roster (418 usos municipalities after post-1995 switching), common-support trimming relies on post-treatment covariates, and Table 5 reports an unexplained sample size discrepancy (412 treated + 228 control = 640 municipalities).
measurement_bias: Low risk for primary infrastructure outcomes (standardized, uniform INEGI national census and intercensal population count household enumerations across both usos and party municipalities), though Moderate concern applies to unvalidated subjective perception items in the auxiliary 2009 survey (Table 1).
confounding: Serious risk: Although first-differences remove time-invariant municipal unobservables, the propensity score model conditions on multiple post-1995 variables measured after the 1995 constitutional reform (2000 census per-capita GDP residuals, 2000 locality territorial concentration, 1990-2010 average indigenous-language share, 1990-2000 religious/ethnic fractionalization, and contemporaneous spatial lag of neighboring usos status). Baseline public-good coverage levels and pre-1995 trends (e.g., 1980-1990) are excluded from the propensity score, common support is extremely thin in the top block (212 treated vs. 4 control municipalities in Block 7), and poverty-formula federal infrastructure transfers (FAIS/FISM introduced in 1997) create plausible time-varying confounding and catch-up/ceiling dynamics.
attrition: Low concern for primary public-good outcomes (all 570 Oaxaca municipalities have complete INEGI census/conteo data, with 6 non-usos municipalities excluded solely for common-support trimming, leaving n = 564); Moderate concern / insufficient information for auxiliary survey analyses (Table 1 item sample sizes drop from 568 to 362 without explanation of total sample size or non-response, and Table 5 reports unexplained sample counts of Treated = 412 and Control = 228, summing to 640 > 570 municipalities).
reporting_bias: Moderate risk (no pre-analysis plan/protocol): No pre-registration or study protocol exists. Only one propensity-score specification and kernel matching estimator are presented without robustness checks using strictly pre-treatment covariates or alternative matching/panel estimators; narrative conclusions overstate mixed results across four overlapping time windows and two functional forms (e.g., claiming faster education/literacy gains based on one p < 0.10 estimate out of eight cells, and emphasizing sub-period sewerage %Delta gains despite null 1990-2010 effects); and Tables 2-5 contain typesetting omissions of minus signs and inconsistent sample counts.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: Formal municipal governance status (usos y costumbres vs. political party elections under Oaxaca's 1995 constitutional reform) is grounded in official state electoral law and institutional rules (including fiscal transfer rules under FAIS/FISM). However, heterogeneous customary practices are collapsed into a static binary indicator fixed at the post-2000 count (418 usos municipalities), ignoring pre-1995 de facto customary governance and 1995-2000 regime switchers even when evaluating 1990-2000 changes.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: Household water and sewerage access are derived from objective, standardized national census/conteo enumerations (INEGI 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010), ensuring consistent administrative coverage measurement across municipalities, but the paper reports only coarse municipal household coverage percentages without specifying exact census definitions (e.g., piped connection vs. public tap, network sewerage vs. septic tank) or water/sanitation service quality, continuity, or potability, and percentage rate-of-change (%Delta) metrics are highly sensitive to near-zero baseline denominators.
where_found: Research design and identification overview in Summary and Section 1 ([PDF Pages 1–2]) and Section 2 ([PDF Pages 3–4]); institutional comparison and auxiliary 2009 survey cross-tabulation in Section 3 ([PDF Pages 4–7], Table 1); propensity score matching methodology and covariate definitions in Section 4 ([PDF Pages 7–8]); balance tests, matched first-differences ATT estimates for water/sewerage/electricity/illiteracy, and electoral/civic estimates in Section 5 ([PDF Pages 8–11], Tables 2–5, Fig. 2); methodological footnotes in Notes ([PDF Pages 12–13]).

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative field and documentary case study (stakeholder interviews, CMA public participation meeting and informal 'stoep' observations, and comparative local narratives in the Breede-Overberg Water Management Area, South Africa)
why_tool_chosen: The paper reports primary qualitative empirical fieldwork—specifically dated interviews with local councillors, a small-scale farmer, a water board respondent, and a WMA consultant (2001-2004), direct observations of DWAF/CMA public participation meetings and informal 'stoep' interactions, and comparative documentary/field narratives in the Breede-Overberg WMA (supplemented by 2003-2004 fieldwork noted in Footnote 17)—with no quantitative analysis or systematic review protocol. It therefore fits the CASP Qualitative Checklist for primary qualitative field/documentary case studies.
overall_rating: High methodological concern (4 Can't tell and 2 No items out of 9 scored CASP criteria)
selection_bias: High concern — The two Breede-Overberg case narratives (Ruensveld/Duivenhoks commercial farmers vs. Kassiesbaai fishing village) were purposively chosen to illustrate contrasting social networks (PDF Page 4, Section 4, p. 198), and the paper reports zero sampling frame, inclusion criteria, sample size, or recruitment strategy for interview respondents or observed CMA meetings.
measurement_bias: High concern — No interview guide, observation protocol, audio-recording or transcription procedure, language/translation handling, or researcher reflexivity is reported, creating substantial risk of observer and social-desirability bias when assessing sensitive constructs such as shame, ignorance, and institutional distrust across sharp racial and technocratic divides.
confounding: Not applicable / Uncontrolled (qualitative comparative case narrative without causal identification) — Historical apartheid privilege, racial classification, income/time resources, literacy/numeracy, and geographic context differ simultaneously between the Ruensveld/Duivenhoks commercial farming areas and Kassiesbaai, though the author qualitatively notes competing explanations for non-participation such as household poverty priorities (jobs, housing, education) and potential trust in the ANC state (PDF Page 9 Footnote 11, p. 203; PDF Page 13 Section 6.5, p. 207).
attrition: Can't tell / No information — Because the total number of interviewees, invited stakeholders, and observed meetings across 2001-2004 is never reported, study non-response or participant drop-out cannot be evaluated (though low attendance by marginalized residents at public participation forums is substantively noted on PDF Page 13, Section 6.5, p. 207).
reporting_bias: High concern — With no Methods section, no inventory of interviews or observed meetings, and no transparent qualitative coding framework, brief illustrative excerpts from five interviews and three CMA meeting utterances (2001-2004) are selectively woven into theoretical commentary, leaving high risk of selective quotation and confirmation bias.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (descriptive statutory and institutional framing) — Accurately identifies the post-apartheid legal architecture governing water resources and services, including the National Water Act (Act 36 of 1998, Schedule 6(1)(l) and Chapter 2, Part 1, Section 5(3)), the Water Services Act (Act 108 of 1997), the 1996 Cabinet abolition of riparian water rights, historical Soil Conservation Act (No. 48 of 1946) networks, and Catchment Management Agency (CMA) / Water User Association (WUA) mandates across 19 Water Management Areas (PDF Pages 2-5, 8-10, pp. 196-199, 202-204), though legal rules are summarized narratively rather than systematically coded.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — Governance outcomes (trust, voice, agency, shame) and local water service conditions (poor water taste/scarcity in Kassiesbaai, lack of water at farm schools cited from a 1999 basin report, and commercial pipeline network metrics cited from secondary history) rely on isolated illustrative quotes and secondary anecdotes without standardized or systematic measurement across households or forums.
where_found: Aims and statutory context in Abstract and Sections 1.1-2 ([PDF Pages 1-3 of 18], pp. 195-197); comparative Breede-Overberg narratives (Ruensveld/Duivenhoks and Kassiesbaai) with primary interviews and secondary history in Section 4 ([PDF Pages 4-8 of 18], pp. 198-202); CMA meeting observations, 'stoep' ethnography, and interviews with officials, consultants, small-scale farmers, and councillors in Sections 6-7 ([PDF Pages 9-15 of 18], pp. 203-209) and Footnote 17 ([PDF Pages 15-16 of 18], pp. 209-210); synthesis in Section 8 ([PDF Page 16 of 18], p. 210). No standalone Methods section is present.

study_design_identified: Systematic review (thematic narrative synthesis of 28 cross-sectional quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods empirical studies; no meta-analysis)
why_tool_chosen: S438 is a secondary systematic review featuring a structured multi-database Boolean search strategy, explicit eligibility criteria, a PRISMA-style screening flow diagram (1,643 initial records to 28 included studies), and formal study quality assessment, making AMSTAR 2 the exact required instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 (with meta-analysis items Q11, Q12, and Q15 marked Not applicable because synthesis is purely thematic/narrative).
overall_rating: Critically Low
selection_bias: High concern (literature searching and screening were not performed in duplicate by two independent reviewers, search dates were omitted, full-text inclusion was restricted to English without methodological justification, 13 excluded full-text papers were not listed, and several included primary studies used convenience or snowball sampling, pp. 3-5, 16, 18).
measurement_bias: Moderate to high concern (data extraction was not reported as performed in duplicate, and definitions of water supply reliability, coping strategies, time valuation, and coping cost units varied substantially across primary studies without standardized measurement criteria, pp. 2, 13, 16).
confounding: High concern (all 28 included primary studies were cross-sectional, and the review's generic summed quality score in Table 1 did not evaluate control for confounding in primary analyses of socio-economic, tenure, or reliability determinants).
attrition: Not applicable / Unclear (secondary systematic review of 28 cross-sectional primary studies with no longitudinal follow-up; however, 13 full-text exclusions in Figure 1 lack an itemized list with study-specific exclusion reasons).
reporting_bias: High concern (no pre-registered review protocol or pre-analysis plan was reported, publication bias was not formally assessed in the narrative synthesis despite searching first 50 Google/Google Scholar hits for grey literature, and findings from high-risk-of-bias studies were integrated uncritically alongside low-risk studies).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / Descriptive only (legal, regulatory, and institutional variables—such as land tenure, illegal network connections, mandatory fixed utility tariffs during supply interruptions, and fragmented or absent regulation of private wells and water vendors—were not systematically coded or verified against primary legal sources, appearing only as narrative observations drawn from included studies on pp. 10, 12-13, and 16).
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate concern (household coping strategies were systematically organized into 15 actions across 5 thematic categories in Table 3, but coping costs, water quantities, willingness to pay, and health/water-quality outcomes relied on heterogeneous, mostly self-reported cross-sectional measures without duplicate extraction verification, pp. 10-16).
where_found: Methods in Sections 2.1-2.4 (PDF pp. 2-4); screening flowchart Figure 1 and risk-of-bias Table 1 in Section 3 (PDF pp. 4-6); study characteristics in Table 2 (PDF pp. 7-9) and coping strategies matrix in Table 3 (PDF p. 11); thematic synthesis in Sections 3.1-3.5 (PDF pp. 10-14); limitations, regulatory context, and heterogeneity discussion in Section 4 (PDF pp. 15-17); Author Contributions and Conflicts of Interest on PDF p. 18.

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative participatory study (community-based participatory action research using photovoice, structured group discussions, and phenomenological analysis)
why_tool_chosen: The study collects and analyzes exclusively qualitative primary empirical data—participant-generated photographs, Chichewa gallery-walk discussions structured by the PHOTO guide, and phenomenological thematic interpretation—with no quantitative comparator or statistical component (Table 1 merely catalogs photo counts and titles across themes). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the required appraisal tool for primary qualitative designs.
overall_rating: Low-to-moderate methodological concern (9 Yes, 0 Can't tell / No items across Q1-Q9; minor concerns regarding small health-center-recruited sample, unreported transcription/translation mechanics, and local leaders' unplanned workshop presence)
selection_bias: Moderate concern (inherent to small purposive participatory design): 8 women (4 postpartum mothers and 4 female guardians, aged 20-43) were purposively selected from two high-vulnerability health facility catchment areas (Chimvu and Thekerani) in Thyolo District in consultation with local health centers based on recent facility delivery, availability, and willingness to share with outsiders, which suits exploratory photovoice inquiry but excludes mothers delivering outside facilities or unable to attend workshops and limits broader transferability.
measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: participant-led photography, Chichewa-language PHOTO group discussions, co-researcher captioning, and community exhibition validation strengthen credibility, but the unplanned attendance of three local leaders during workshops introduces potential authority/social-desirability bias, and the paper does not report whether Chichewa discussions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, or back-translated.
confounding: Not applicable in causal/statistical terms (primary qualitative phenomenological study with no quantitative effect estimation); contextual seasonal, environmental, household, and gendered socio-cultural factors shaping postpartum water access and workload are explored narratively.
attrition: Low concern: eligibility required availability for the full study duration, and all 8 enrolled co-researchers completed training, 5-day photo collection (281 total photographs across the two groups), gallery-walk selection, and group dialogue sessions, although pre-enrollment refusal counts during health-center candidate identification are not reported.
reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: no pre-registered qualitative protocol is cited, but the authors transparently report how 281 photographs were narrowed by co-researchers to 44 images (Table 1), include voices from all 8 coded co-researchers alongside community validation, and explicitly explain privacy-based exclusion of identifiable faces or sensitive images.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / incidental (not a legal-empirical study): formal law and policy (such as the Government of Malawi's 2022 Revised National Water Policy and women's exclusion from formal water governance structures) appear only as background framing, while primary empirical observations capture informal village household water-separation rules, gendered domestic and school/facility labor norms, and collective community well-digging practices via participant narratives.
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for qualitative lived-experience inquiry, weak for clinical or microbiological outcomes: household water acquisition barriers, queueing, seasonal river hazards, rationing trade-offs, psychosocial stress, and infant/maternal hygiene compromises are richly documented through 44 selected photographs and narratives across all 8 co-researchers, whereas water contamination and maternal/newborn health conditions (e.g., cholera, infections, rashes) rely on self-reported perceptions rather than objective clinical or water-quality testing.
where_found: Study design, setting, purposive recruitment criteria, researcher reflexivity, photovoice workshops, phenomenological NVivo 12 analysis, community validation, and ethics are reported in Abstract (PDF Page 1), Section 2 Methods (PDF Pages 2-4), and Ethics statement (PDF Page 13); thematic findings, photo counts (Table 1), and captioned verbatim narratives appear in Section 3 Results (PDF Pages 4-12); methodological limitations and transferability are discussed in Section 4 Discussion (PDF Pages 12-13).

study_design_identified: Cross-national longitudinal macro-panel observational regression (two-way country and year fixed-effects Prais-Winsten GLS panel analysis of 135 low- and middle-income countries, nominally 1990-2015) without a discrete policy/intervention comparator
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies covers quantitative cross-sectional surveys and observational regressions without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Although the dataset has a country-year panel structure (nominally 1990-2015), the study evaluates general macroeconomic and governance correlates rather than a discrete policy or intervention with treatment/control arms (ruling out ROBINS-I) and models aggregate ecological prevalence of rural water coverage rather than following exposed and unexposed cohorts initially free of an incident outcome (ruling out JBI Cohort Studies).
overall_rating: High concern
selection_bias: Some to High concern: Country eligibility is defined by objective World Bank 2015 GNI per capita thresholds (Tables A1-A3, PDF pp. 18-19; noting a minor discrepancy between 51 lower-middle-income countries stated on PDF p. 4 and 50 listed in Table A2), but classifying countries across 1990-2015 using end-of-period 2015 income groups conditions subgroup stratification on post-baseline economic performance, and heavy unaddressed country-year missingness selects toward countries and years with complete statistical reporting.
measurement_bias: High concern: While economic and water variables come from standard World Bank, UNESCO, OECD, and WHO/UNICEF JMP databases, the six governance exposures are discretized into dummy categories whose numerical cutoffs are omitted from Figure 2 (PDF p. 10), WGI temporal variation may reflect changing data sources rather than actual governance shifts (PDF p. 10), female primary completion rate is an unadjusted gross intake proxy that ignores final-year dropouts and can exceed 100% (PDF p. 8), and aggregate JMP access percentages do not capture supply regularity or water quality (PDF p. 2).
confounding: High concern: Although country and year fixed effects, World Bank income-group stratification, and 1-period lags on female primary completion and ODA are used (Sections 2.2 and 2.4, PDF pp. 5-9), severe residual confounding remains: global regressions (Tables 2-4) enter LogGNI, Female, and Agriculture one at a time in separate equations due to multicollinearity (reintroducing omitted-variable bias), subgroup models (Tables 5-7) drop governance covariates via preliminary Wald tests, 1-year lags do not resolve simultaneity, and major time-varying confounders (domestic public WASH spending, urbanization, conflict, climatic shocks) are unmeasured.

measurement_bias: Moderate to high risk: Standardized regulatory tariffs and EU water-testing metrics are objective, but 'organizational costs' (OC) are collapsed into four ordinal levels without disclosing Euro cut-offs and suffer from systematic accounting asymmetry (municipal bureaucracies omit shared town-hall overhead prior to Law 194/2009, whereas PPPs and municipal corporations internalize full costs), and raw complaint counts (Comp) are not normalized per customer/connection and conflate tariff-hike complaints with operational service failures (Sections 4.1 and 5, PDF Pages 4, 6-7).
confounding: High risk: No design or statistical controls are implemented for major municipal confounders (population/customer base size, urban vs. rural density, hydrological/topographical cost drivers, network age/leakage, baseline municipal fiscal stress driving PPP adoption, or concession contract stage), nor are property, management model, and organizational costs mutually adjusted for one another (Sections 4.3 and 5, PDF Pages 5-8).
attrition: Low risk: Cross-sectional census of all 308 Portuguese municipalities with 100% completeness (308/308) on tariff and institutional variables and 96.4% completeness (297/308) on complaint and water-quality variables, though the 11 missing municipalities on quality metrics are not explained (Table 1, PDF Page 4).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan exists, subgroup sample sizes across the two property categories, five management models, and four organizational cost brackets are never tabulated, and subgroup means are reported selectively in prose while omitting subgroup distributions for water-quality compliance (PaV) across management models despite a statistically significant omnibus ANOVA (p = .000 in Table 3, PDF Page 7).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate: Statutory governance categories (Municipal, Inter-municipal and Regional Corporations Act of 1998; Decree-Law 86/2003; Decree-Law 194/2009; EU Directive 2000/60/CE) and the five Portuguese water delivery models are grounded in national law and ERSAR regulatory classifications, but dichotomizing municipal concessions as private 'property' conflates delegated management with asset ownership, and treating five unordered institutional models as a linear 1-to-5 scale in correlations and linearity tests distorts legal measurement (Sections 3, 4.1, 4.3, and Table 5, PDF Pages 3-8).
outcome_measurement_quality: Mixed (strong for tariffs and water quality compliance; weak for complaints): Domestic tariff bills at 60, 120, and 180 m3 (CP'60, CP'120, CP'180) and EU-mandated parametric sample completion (PaT) and drinking-water compliance (PaV) come from mandatory, standardized ERSAR regulatory reporting, whereas service quality is proxied by raw annual complaint counts (Comp, range 0-291) unadjusted for population served and confounded by price dissatisfaction (Section 4.1, Table 1, PDF Page 4; Section 5, PDF Page 6).

study_design_identified: Convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional study combining a descriptive household survey (target n=630 across two rounds), sanitary/microbial/chlorine water quality and GIS/DEM assessments, and semi-structured qualitative interviews with utility technicians, managers, and board community representatives across 10 small towns
why_tool_chosen: The study explicitly employs a primary mixed-methods cross-sectional design ('employing both quantitative and qualitative methods', PDF Page 3) that integrates quantitative descriptive data (household survey, WHO sanitary inspection scores, microbial/chlorine tests, DEM flood risk) with qualitative semi-structured interviews (utility technicians, managers, and Water Board community representatives) across six domains of the How tough is WASH framework, with no randomized or quasi-experimental comparator. overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (per MMAT 2018 narrative guidance, no numeric score; strong mixed-methods integration [5.1-5.4 Yes], but overall quality is constrained by weaknesses in qualitative substantiation [1.4 No; 1.3 Can't tell] and quantitative representativeness and reporting transparency [4.2 No; 4.4-4.5 Can't tell; 5.5 No])
selection_bias: High concern: Study towns (n=10) were purposively selected from two climate-vulnerable zones in Oromia and Somali regions (PDF Page 4). Within towns, simple random sampling of households was restricted to utility customer lists of households already using piped water (PDF Page 4), systematically excluding unserved/unpiped town residents—up to 80% of households in towns such as Aweday where piped coverage was only 20% (PDF Pages 2-3).
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Physical and water-quality measurements used recognized tools—WHO sanitary inspection checklists, membrane filtration for microbial CFU/100 mL, Palintest DPD visual color comparator for free residual chlorine, and ArcGIS Digital Elevation Modeling for flood risk (PDF Pages 4-5). confounding: Not applicable / Uncontrolled descriptive design: The study is purely descriptive and makes no causal effect estimates; the authors explicitly note that no statistical associations between coliform levels and sanitary risks were explored, and no multivariable adjustment for town- or household-level confounders was conducted (PDF Pages 5-6).
attrition: Can't tell / Moderate concern: Data were collected in two rounds (August and December 2022) with a planned sample of 630 households assuming a 10% non-response rate (PDF Page 4, Table 1), but the paper never reports actual household response rates, achieved sample sizes in either round, or between-round attrition. reporting_bias: High concern (selective/incomplete descriptive reporting): Although 630 households were sampled across 10 towns and two seasonal rounds (August and December 2022; PDF Pages 3-4), no socio-demographic table, response rate, town-level survey table, or seasonal comparison between August and December rounds is reported; only isolated summary percentages appear in prose (PDF Pages 7-8). outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Water supply resilience outcomes combined objective physical/microbial tests (CFU/100 mL at source, DPD free residual chlorine, WHO sanitary inspection, DEM flood vulnerability in Table 2) with subjective household and key-informant perceptions. study_design_identified: Retrospective non-randomized comparative administrative evaluation (cohort of failed onsite wastewater treatment systems followed for 120-day Notice of Violation compliance, analyzed via unadjusted and multivariable logistic regression)
why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I is the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because S331 is a non-randomized empirical evaluation of an administrative/regulatory intervention—Point-of-Sale (POS) OWTS inspection—against a genuine active comparator group (non-POS O&M inspections: annual aeration, newly installed 12-month, nuisance complaint, and stormwater IDDE inspections), following failed OWTSs forward from BOH Notice of Violation issuance over a defined 120-day compliance window. Unlike a cross-sectional prevalence study (JBI Analytical Cross Sectional) or a non-intervention etiological exposure study (JBI Cohort), the dissertation explicitly frames POS inspection as a regulatory O&M program tool whose effectiveness on compliance timeliness is being evaluated.
overall_rating: Serious
selection_bias: Serious concern: From 1,751 extracted PCHD inspection records (Jan 2, 2015 – June 30, 2023), 481 (27.5%) were excluded during initial cleanup (duplicates, missing PINs/addresses, incomplete/ambiguous reports, or out-of-window dates), 46 failed voluntary inspections were excluded due to indeterminable POS/non-POS status, and 83 of 1,021 failed OWTS cases (8.1%) were excluded from multivariable regression (n = 938) because they lacked complete data on post-inspection remediation covariates (new system type, repair vs. replacement, correction cost, or system age), likely excluding uncorrected non-compliant systems and conditioning inclusion on post-exposure remediation progress.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Exposure (POS vs. non-POS inspection) and outcome (compliance within 120 days of BOH NOV) were extracted from routine PCHD administrative databases (HDIS, GIS, digital/scanned files), avoiding recall bias, but 46 failed 'voluntary inspections' could not be classified as POS or non-POS, PCHD environmental health staff (the author's own agency) were unblinded to inspection context when signing off compliance, and exact endpoint operationalization (installation date vs. final inspection vs. document completion) has minor definitional ambiguity.
confounding: Serious concern: The study relies on observational logistic regression without quasi-experimental identification and omits major socioeconomic and transactional confounders (household income, wealth/savings, property value, real-estate sale liquidity/escrow arrangements, and baseline failure severity), as explicitly acknowledged on p. 76 (PDF p. 93). Furthermore, three of the four adjusted covariates (new system type used for correction, repair vs. replacement, and correction cost) are post-inspection remediation variables affected by the POS context rather than true baseline confounders.
attrition: Serious concern (missing administrative data / complete-case exclusions): Although the June 30, 2023 cutoff provided at least 120 days of post-NOV follow-up, 83 of 1,021 classified failed OWTS records (8.1%) were dropped from the logistic regression models (n = 938) via complete-case deletion due to missing covariate data, alongside 46 unclassified voluntary inspection failures (4.3%) and an unspecified share of 481 initially rejected database records with incomplete/ambiguous reports, with no missingness comparison or sensitivity analysis.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan exists. The author reports data-driven model refinement after cleaning ('verifying variable coding, collapsing sparse categories, removing predictors with insufficient data variation', pp. 47-48 / PDF pp. 64-65) and reports regression models only for the dichotomized 120-day 'effective compliance' cutoff despite also defining a 60-day 'restrictive compliance' window and framing the dissertation title around 'compliance duration' without presenting 60-day or continuous survival/time-to-event estimates.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak: The dissertation cites the governing Ohio statutory and administrative rules (ORC Chapter 3718 / 3718.02 and OAC Chapter 3701-29) and PCHD's two-stage 60-day plus 60-day (120-day) Board of Health NOV enforcement procedure, but contains a direct internal contradiction on Portage County's own legal rule—stating on p. 24 (PDF p. 41) that PCHD has NOT adopted a mandatory POS program (offering a voluntary option and not stopping property sales upon failure), yet asserting on p. 84 (PDF p. 101) that Portage County regulations MANDATE POS inspection and repair/replacement prior to property transfer. It also pools four legally distinct non-POS inspection regimes (annual Class I ATU/NPDES, 12-month newly installed OWTS, nuisance complaint, and MS4 stormwater IDDE) into one binary reference group.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate (adequate for administrative compliance, limited for physical sanitation quality): The outcome captures binary administrative compliance (faulty OWTS correction within <=120 days vs. >120 days after BOH NOV) from local health district enforcement records rather than physical effluent or water-quality measurements, collapses continuous compliance duration into a single 120-day dichotomy, and does not distinguish delayed corrections (>120 days) from permanently uncorrected systems.
where_found: Primary methods, variable definitions, data cleaning exclusions, and regression specifications are in Definitions (pp. xii-xvii; [PDF Pages 12-17 of 153]) and Chapter 3: Research Methodology (pp. 29-50; Table 1, Figures 1-4; [PDF Pages 46-67 of 153]). Descriptive statistics (n = 1,021), complete-case regression results (n = 938), and VIF diagnostics are in Chapter 4: Results (pp. 53-71; Tables 2-5; [PDF Pages 70-88 of 153]). Local legal/enforcement context, differential incremental-repair rules, and acknowledgment of omitted socioeconomic confounders are in Chapter 1 (pp. 5-7; [PDF Pages 22-24 of 153]), Chapter 2 (p. 24; [PDF Page 41 of 153]), and Chapter 5: Discussion (pp. 72-86; [PDF Pages 89-103 of 153]; note text past PDF Page 103 including Appendices A-B was truncated in prompt delivery, though all core empirical chapters were readable in full).

study_design_identified: Single-country institutional and political-economy historical case study synthesizing secondary survey, water-quality, and statutory/regulatory sources (no primary empirical data collection or systematic literature search)
why_tool_chosen: The paper explicitly frames itself as a single-country institutional-historical case study of urban water governance and access in Ghana (1957-2011), tracing public utility restructuring (GWSC to GWCL), PPP contract selection (AVRL 2005-2011 management contract), and statutory regulation (PURC Act 538, 1997) alongside secondary empirical evidence. It fits none of the six conventional empirical checklists: there is no randomization (RoB 2), no comparator arm or quasi-experimental design (single-case histories without a comparator cannot be assigned to ROBINS-I), no primary cross-sectional or cohort dataset analysed (JBI), no primary qualitative fieldwork/interviews (CASP/MMAT), and no systematic search protocol (AMSTAR 2 is prohibited for non-systematic narrative reviews). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework directly matches this institutional/legal-historical case study design while capturing its secondary-source selection, confounding, and statutory accuracy limitations.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: High methodological concern for causal/empirical inference (strong conceptual outcome framing, jurisdictional specificity, and institutional context; adequate exposure classification and secondary measurement reporting; weak legal citation precision, sampling/selection transparency, causal identification, confounding control, replication potential, and reflexivity; coding not assessable)
selection_bias: High concern — Purposive choice of Ghana as an illustrative national case is explicitly justified, but there is no documented search strategy or selection protocol governing which secondary surveys, scientific studies, dissertations, and media reports within Ghana were included or excluded.
measurement_bias: Moderate to high concern — Establishes a clear multidimensional distinction between wide coverage and deep access (quality, reliability, cost, equitable distribution) using cited secondary metrics, but relies uncritically on heterogeneous secondary sources (including operator web pages, unpublished theses, and news portals) without auditing primary measurement validity or sample denominators.
confounding: High concern — Mentions historical infrastructure decay and debt from the 1970s-1980s, rapid urbanisation (from ~30% to >40% between 1990 and 2008), population/tourism/industrial demand growth, and bi-directional neighbourhood-income poverty, but uses no analytical or empirical strategy to disentangle these confounders from commercialisation or the 2005-2011 AVRL management contract.
attrition: Not assessable — Secondary single-country institutional case study synthesizing published cross-sectional surveys, scientific water-quality studies, and historical accounts with no primary cohort or participant follow-up.
reporting_bias: High concern — No pre-specified protocol, literature search strategy, or source-inclusion rules; narrative assembly of secondary statistics and illustrative examples creates substantial risk of selective reporting aligned with the paper's critique of market-oriented water reform.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak to moderate — Clearly maps PPP contractual forms (Table 1) and institutional restructuring (GWSC to GWCL in 1998, CWSA rural decoupling, PURC creation in 1997, AVRL management contract 2005-2011, GUWCL in 2011), but relies on secondary accounts rather than primary legal/contractual instruments, inconsistently cites the PURC enabling statute as both Act 538 (1997) and Act 578 on the same page (PDF Page 9, p. 1142), and conflates the implemented management contract with affermage in the concluding critique (PDF Page 9, p. 1142).
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate — Strong conceptual disaggregation of urban water outcomes across MDG coverage, microbial/chemical contamination, continuity and per-capita daily volume (litres/day), official tariff versus tanker-market pricing and household expenditure shares, and wealth-quintile/neighbourhood connection equity, but entirely dependent on secondary studies whose primary measurement procedures and sampling frames are not verified.

study_design_identified: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (121 geographic village clusters comprising 332 rural villages across four DRC provinces, stratified block-randomized to 50 intervention clusters and 71 control clusters, assessed at median 3.6 years post-intervention)
why_tool_chosen: The study randomly assigned multi-village geographic clusters (121 clusters containing 332 villages) to a community-driven WASH and local institutional strengthening intervention (50 clusters) or control (71 clusters) and analyzed outcomes at village, household, and child levels. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, a cluster-randomized controlled trial requires the RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant) covering all six official domains (D1a, D1b, D2, D3, D4, D5).
overall_rating: Some concerns
selection_bias: Some concerns: Computerized block randomization of 121 village clusters (339 eligible villages) in Stata was appropriate, but 7 villages were dropped post-randomization (6 randomly to meet operational targets and 1 control village due to a coding error), no baseline survey was conducted before randomization, and all participating households were sampled and recruited post-intervention in unmasked clusters (substantially mitigated by random-walk nth-household selection and restricting eligibility to residents living in the village for at least 4 years, i.e., prior to the intervention).
measurement_bias: Some concerns (domain-specific divergence between objective and self-reported measures): Neither participants nor independent IHfRA enumerators were masked to treatment status. Objective protocols were used for child length-for-age Z-scores (supervisor duplicate checks), E. coli/thermotolerant coliform MPN testing of village water points and household storage containers, observed water point functionality, and 2-hour pre-interview structured handwashing observations, whereas primary 7-day diarrhea, the WASH institutions index, improved water/sanitation access, and water governance perceptions relied on unmasked respondent self-report (with social-desirability reactivity empirically shown by +9 pp self-reported handwashing vs null observed handwashing).
confounding: Low concern: Treatment was randomly assigned at the cluster level by the research team in Stata within 12 province-by-cluster-size randomization blocks, all intention-to-treat regressions included stratum fixed effects (plus child age and sex indicators for child health outcomes), and time-invariant respondent and household characteristics at 3.6 years were well balanced across arms (Table 2), although pre-randomization baseline outcome data were not collected.
attrition: Some concerns: Cluster/village retention at 3.6 years was very high (329 of 332 randomized villages assessed; 99.1%), and 86% of 5-month respondents (1,133/1,312; 88% of households) were re-interviewed at 3.6 years, but 140 longitudinal households (11%) were replaced, 2,142 of 2,374 eligible households (90.2%) contributed valid child length-for-age Z-scores in Table 3, and the absence of pre-intervention baseline data prevents completely ruling out differential post-randomization out-migration (arm-specific flow details in Fig 1 are in an unrendered figure graphic).
reporting_bias: Some concerns: The trial was not prospectively registered prior to the March-June 2018 cluster randomization because no baseline data were collected; initial AEA registration occurred in late 2019 (5-month wave), PACTR registration in February 2021, and the 3.6-year follow-up outcome update and pre-analysis plan were posted in April 2023 at the conclusion of 3.6-year fieldwork (November 2022-February/April 2023), though the authors attest that principal investigators had not seen the 3.6-year data prior to posting and transparently report null primary health results with open microdata and code.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: The DRC national Healthy Villages and Schools governance intervention (seven village norms, 9-step Health Zone-community agreement, elected village WASH committee, and Community Action Plan for Maintenance) is clearly specified, and local institutional persistence was operationalized via a standardized multi-item WASH governance index (committee presence, meeting frequency, non-maintenance expenses, maintenance plan, and community health/hygiene tracking) alongside subjective governance perception items, though institutional index components relied on survey reports rather than independent administrative records.
outcome_measurement_quality: Strong for biophysical and observational WASH/health outcomes; moderate/weak for self-reported access and morbidity: Anthropometry (Salter scales and wall-mounted rods with supervisor re-measurement), microbial drinking water quality (Aquagenx Compartment Bag Test for E. coli and total coliform MPN at sources and household containers), water point functionality (direct observation), and handwashing (2-hour structured observation prior to interviews) were rigorously measured, whereas primary 7-day child diarrhea and household use of JMP-defined improved water and sanitation facilities relied on unmasked self-reports.

study_design_identified: Comparative institutional and legal-historical three-country case study synthesizing secondary literature and statutory/policy trajectories across Nicaragua, Honduras, and Costa Rica (no primary field data collection or systematic review protocol)
why_tool_chosen: The article has no randomized or quasi-experimental intervention comparator (ruling out RoB 2 and ROBINS-I), no cross-sectional or cohort quantitative dataset (ruling out JBI checklists), no primary qualitative fieldwork/interview/ethnographic data collection reported in this paper (ruling out CASP and MMAT), and no systematic literature search or screening protocol (ruling out AMSTAR 2). Because it is explicitly structured as a comparative three-country institutional and legal-historical case study tracing statutory water reforms, decentralization laws, and CBWM governance interfaces across Nicaragua, Honduras, and Costa Rica (PDF pp. 4, 8-13), it directly matches the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework in RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Moderate-to-weak empirical rigor (strong jurisdictional specificity and institutional context; adequate legal source accuracy, exposure definition, and country-case rationale; weak selection process, outcome/measurement transparency, causal identification, confounding control, coding/replication transparency, and reflexivity)
selection_bias: High concern / Weak control: Country case selection (Nicaragua, Honduras, Costa Rica) is purposive and explicitly relies in part on the authors' prior regional research and expertise—omitting other Central American Dry Corridor countries such as Guatemala and El Salvador—while within-country documentary and subnational examples are selected narratively without inclusion or screening criteria (PDF p. 4).
measurement_bias: High concern / Weak control: No primary empirical measurement protocol is used; CBWM counts, registration proportions, and access figures are drawn from heterogeneous secondary academic, NGO, donor, and newspaper sources across varying years, and Note 7 explicitly notes discrepancies in national CBWM estimates due to inconsistent state documentation and unregistered providers (PDF pp. 6, 9, 11-12, 16).
confounding: High concern / Weak control: Historical, macroeconomic, donor, and political confounders (e.g., Nicaragua's 1979 Sandinista Revolution and 1990s neoliberal shift, Costa Rica's 1982 structural adjustment and baseline social spending, USAID/multilateral investment waves, and rural poverty) are discussed narratively, but there is no empirical design or structured comparative control to isolate the effects of legal reforms; the authors explicitly acknowledge difficulty disentangling what shaped CBWM features over time (PDF pp. 8-12).
attrition: Not applicable (comparative institutional and legal-historical case study synthesizing secondary literature and statutory trajectories without a longitudinal cohort or participant sample subject to follow-up loss).
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern / Can't tell: No study protocol, systematic literature search, or structured comparative coding matrix is reported, leaving potential for selective citation of secondary evidence to support the authors' normative policy proposals on state-network collaboration and accountability (PDF pp. 4, 12-15).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Key national water statutes, municipal decentralization laws, regulatory agencies, and CBWM legal recognition rules are coherently traced across Nicaragua (1979 INAA decree, Law 40 of 1988, 2003 Citizen Participation Law, Law 620 of 2007, Law 722 of 2010), Honduras (1990 Law of Municipalities, 2003 General Framework Law for Water and Sanitation), and Costa Rica (Law 218 of 1939, 1997 CAARS and 2000 ASADAS frameworks, proposed 2009 Bill Law 17324), but legal descriptions rely on secondary literature rather than primary statutory texts or official gazettes and omit some decree numbers and systematic doctrinal coding (PDF pp. 8-12, 16-20).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Governance and water provision outcomes—including formal CBWM registration rates, post-construction system maintenance, financial viability, water access inequities, and climate-change vulnerability—are discussed conceptually or illustrated with scattered, non-harmonized secondary statistics from disparate years rather than measured with standardized cross-national indicators (PDF pp. 5-13).
where_found: Case selection rationale and research framing in Introduction (PDF pp. 2-4); regional background and Figure 1 secondary CBWM data in 'Rural water provision at the state-society interface in Latin America' (PDF pp. 4-8); country-specific legal and institutional histories in 'The evolving role of the state in rural water provision' covering Nicaragua (PDF pp. 8-9), Honduras (PDF pp. 9-11), and Costa Rica (PDF pp. 11-12); cross-case thematic comparison in 'Synthesizing the state role in rural water provision across cases' (PDF pp. 12-13); normative policy proposals in 'Reenvisioning the role of the state in rural water provision' (PDF pp. 14-15); methodological/data caveats in Endnotes 1-9 (PDF pp. 15-16).

study_design_identified: Single-city qualitative case study combining documentary/policy review with semi-structured expert interviews (structured policy-ranking elicitation and thematic content categorization) among 12 local water professionals
why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical component consists of 12 individual semi-structured expert interviews contextualized by a narrative literature and policy review in a single municipal setting (Seattle). Although three of the five interview prompts asked respondents to rank policies from a researcher-curated list and tallied rank points (across n=6 to 8 respondents per subsector) alongside frequency counts of coded open-ended themes, there is no quantitative sampling frame, statistical estimation, or distinct quantitative study strand; thus CASP Qualitative Checklist is the appropriate primary qualitative case-study instrument rather than MMAT or ROBINS-I.
overall_rating: High methodological concern (4 Yes, 1 No, 4 Can't tell on Q1-Q9)
selection_bias: High concern: Purposive selection of 12 unnamed 'water professionals familiar with water services and resilience in the Seattle area' with zero reporting of recruitment frame, institutional affiliations, role breakdown, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or refusal rates (PDF Pages 8, 11, Sections 3 and 3.1).
measurement_bias: High concern: Policy importance for resilience is operationalized solely through interviewees' subjective rankings of researcher-curated policy lists—retaining incomplete rankings and tied placements in point sums without normalization—and single-pass thematic grouping of open-ended answers with no reported recording/transcription protocol or inter-coder reliability check (PDF Pages 9-10, Sections 3 and 3.1).
confounding: High concern (uncontrolled qualitative design): No counterfactual comparator or causal adjustment is attempted; the authors acknowledge that policies operate in interdependent chains alongside environmental shocks, pricing, and informal norms, preventing isolation of any single law's effect on resilience (PDF Pages 8, 10-11, Sections 2 and 3.1).
attrition: Low / Partial item non-response: Single-wave cross-sectional interviews with 12 participants involved no longitudinal panel attrition, but subsector participation varied by self-selection (8 water supply, 6 wastewater, 8 stormwater) and 4 of 12 interviewees ranked fewer than the requested 5 or 10 policies (PDF Page 9, Section 3).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: No study protocol, interview guide appendix, or full candidate policy list is published, and qualitative findings are compressed into theme counts and summary bullet tables without any verbatim participant quotations or discussion of dissenting views (PDF Pages 9-24, Sections 3-6).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak to moderate: The study identifies concrete federal, state, and local instruments (e.g., 1972 Clean Water Act, NPDES permits, 2013 CSO/SSO Consent Decree, 2009 Seattle Stormwater Code, SPU Director's Rules), but groups binding statutes together with capital plans, programs, and historic land purchases without formal statutory citations, doctrinal verification, or enforcement data, and mislabels/misdates the federal Safe Drinking Water Act as the 'National Safe Water Act (1972)' (PDF Pages 10, 15, 18-19, Sections 3.1 and 4.2).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (perceptual only): Primary outcomes are water professionals' subjective perceptions of which policies enable resilience and perceived future challenges, rather than objective empirical measures of service continuity, CSO frequency, water quality compliance, or shock recovery (PDF Pages 7-9, 11-23, Sections 2, 3, and 4-6).

study_design_identified: Observational longitudinal country-year dynamic panel econometric study (44 Sub-Saharan African countries, 2002-2015) using two-step system Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) with internal lagged instruments
why_tool_chosen: The study estimates the direct impact of institutional governance quality on access to improved sanitation across a comparative longitudinal panel of 44 countries (2002-2015) using dynamic panel system-GMM internal instrumental-variable estimation and policy counterfactuals (e.g., DR Congo vs. Mauritius). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, ROBINS-I is the designated instrument for non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel and IV-type econometric evaluations of policy/institutional exposures.
overall_rating: Serious
selection_bias: Moderate risk: The sample includes 44 Sub-Saharan African countries over 2002-2015 selected on data availability (excluding several SSA states and missing country-years, with the country list deferred to online Appendix B), creating potential under-representation of fragile or conflict-affected jurisdictions lacking governance, aid, or sanitation statistics.
measurement_bias: Serious risk: Institutional exposures rely on subjective perception-based WGI composites vulnerable to halo effects and reverse causality from broader economic and public-service performance, while sanitation outcomes rely on highly persistent interpolated national/rural/urban aggregate series (first-lag correlation of 0.99).
confounding: Serious risk: Benchmark two-step system-GMM regressions treat institutional quality as strictly exogenous and omit time fixed effects; several specifications (Tables 2, 3, and 6) yield explosive lagged dependent variable coefficients exceeding 1.0, and specifications treating institutions as endogenous via internal lags suffer from instrument proliferation (country-to-instrument ratio r < 1). As the authors explicitly state on p. 17, the aggregate design does not establish causality.
attrition: Moderate risk: In an unbalanced panel of 44 countries over 14 years (616 potential country-years), baseline models retain 541 observations (~12% missing) and models with foreign aid and FDI retain 513 observations (~17% missing). Forward orthogonal deviations are used to mitigate observation loss from panel gaps, but patterns and causes of missing country-years are not analyzed.
reporting_bias: No information (no pre-analysis plan or protocol exists), though selective reporting concern is partially mitigated by extensive sensitivity reporting across all six WGI dimensions, percentile ranks, three composite indices, domestic vs. foreign control sets, time fixed effects, endogenous GMM specifications, and rural/urban splits (Tables 2-9).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / low specificity: Legal and institutional variables (including Rule of Law and Regulatory Quality) are operationalized solely via aggregate Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) subjective perception scores (-2.5 to 2.5 and percentile ranks) rather than coding formal sanitation statutes, regulatory agencies, or de jure legal rules; as acknowledged on p. 13 (citing Rodrik 2004), WGI captures investor and survey perceptions rather than specific formal institutional designs.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / macro-standardized only: Access to improved sanitation (AIS) is consistently defined across national, rural, and urban series as the percentage of the population with access to and using improved sanitation facilities, but relies on smoothed aggregate country-year statistics (lag-1 correlation = 0.99) without household-level verification of facility functionality or explicit primary database citations in the main text (deferred to online Appendix).
where_found: Full text of the 18-page published article read: Abstract & Section I Introduction (PDF pp. 1-4); Section II Data and Variables of Interest & Table 1 (PDF pp. 4-7); Section III Estimation Procedure (PDF pp. 7-8); Section IV Results & Robustness Regressions, Tables 2-7 (PDF pp. 8-14); Section V Rural versus Urban Analysis, Tables 8-9 (PDF pp. 14-16); Section VI Concluding Remarks (PDF pp. 16-17). study_design_identified: Primary qualitative case study combining qualitative content analysis of 10 policy documents (1995-2020) with 37 semi-structured interviews (31 interviewees) and 1 focus group (5 participants) in the Middle Draa Valley, Morocco
why_tool_chosen: Section 2 (Methods, PDF pp. 3-5) establishes that this is a purely qualitative primary empirical study combining qualitative content analysis of 10 policy documents with 37 semi-structured field interviews and 1 focus group, with no quantitative analytical component (Table 1 reports interviewee counts only). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the designated instrument for primary qualitative studies using interviews, focus groups, and qualitative documentary/field case methods.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (8 Yes, 1 No, 1 Can't tell on Q1-Q9; valuable qualitative contribution on Q10)
selection_bias: Moderate concern — Purposeful sampling of government agencies and snowball plus maximal variation sampling of inhabitants are well-suited to qualitative inquiry (PDF p. 4), but one of the six oases (Mezguita) was excluded without explanation (PDF p. 3), individual interviews were heavily male-skewed (26 men vs. 5 women, partially offset by one 5-woman focus group; Table 1, PDF p. 4), and several core policy plans were inaccessible in full official form (PDF p. 3, Appendix A).
measurement_bias: Moderate concern — Interview guides (Appendices C-D) and deductive coding rules in MAXQDA (Appendix B) are transparent and French-to-English policy quote translations were double-checked by a certified native speaker (PDF p. 5), but Amazigh/Darija interview translations lacked reported back-translation, some interviews were not audio-recorded (PDF p. 4), inter-coder reliability procedures were not detailed, and researcher reflexivity was unaddressed despite sensitive disclosures of illegal well-digging and bribery (PDF pp. 4, 17).
confounding: Not applicable as a statistical causal domain (high concern if interpreted causally) — This qualitative case study does not estimate counterfactual treatment effects; links between national water/agricultural subsidies and local aquifer depletion or inequality rely on stakeholder accounts, institutional process-tracing, and secondary literature without controlling for concurrent climatic or market trends (PDF pp. 15-21).
attrition: Low concern / Not applicable (cross-sectional qualitative design) — No longitudinal follow-up was planned across the Feb-Mar 2020 and Oct-Dec 2021 fieldwork periods; however, snowball recruitment refusal or non-response rates are not reported (Can't tell for recruitment refusals; PDF pp. 3-5).
reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern — Findings from both policy document coding (Table 2, Figure 2) and multi-actor interviews are systematically presented alongside the document list, deductive codebook, and interview guides (Appendices A-D, PDF pp. 24-25), though inductive code frequencies are not tabulated and secondary government presentations substituted for non-public national water plans (PDF p. 3).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — Enacted water statutes (Loi No. 10-95 and Loi No. 36-15), administrative drip-irrigation subsidy procedures, ministerial mandates, and customary oasis water-turn (nouba/kharouba) and tribal land-use certification rules are clearly described (PDF pp. 14, 17-18, 24); however, key executive policy plans (PNEEI 2007, National Water Plans, 2020-2027 plan) were not publicly accessible, forcing reliance on official website summaries and officials' conference presentations/articles (PDF p. 3, Appendix A p. 24).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate (qualitative/perceptual only) — Drinking water intermittency, irrigation shortfalls, salinization, groundwater depletion, and water conflicts are assessed via respondent perceptions and cited secondary hydrological/remote-sensing studies rather than primary physical or household measurements, and the authors explicitly did not collect data linking water rights to farm size (PDF pp. 13-18).
