study_design_identified: Single-town mixed-methods case study combining quantitative descriptive GIS spatial analysis (2000 Census demographics and geo-coded municipal/ETJ, zoning, sewer, and highway records) with qualitative participant observation and documentary content analysis of town council deliberations
why_tool_chosen: The authors explicitly employ a mixed-methods primary case study design ('a case study approach and a mix of quantitative and qualitative research methods', [PDF Page 1]) that integrates quantitative descriptive GIS spatial mapping of 2000 Census data and geo-coded public infrastructure/boundary files with qualitative participant observation and content analysis of town council deliberations and planning records. MMAT (using Qualitative 1.1-1.5, Quantitative descriptive 4.1-4.5, and Mixed Methods 5.1-5.5) is therefore the exact matching instrument. ROBINS-I is inappropriate because this is a single-town case history with no quasi-experimental intervention comparator arm, and the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework applies only when a study fits none of the conventional empirical designs.
overall_rating: High methodological concern (weakest-component limitation: Mixed Methods 5.5 rated No, with four Can't tell ratings in Qualitative 1.2-1.5, two Can't tell ratings in Quantitative descriptive 4.4-4.5, and one Can't tell rating in Mixed Methods 5.4; no numeric score computed per MMAT 2018 guidance)
selection_bias: High concern for purposive case and documentary selection: Mebane, NC is a purposively selected single-town case with active environmental justice complaints (WERA 1999 Title VI complaint, [PDF Page 17]); while GIS layers cover the entire town and ETJ, qualitative cases, council minutes, and personal communications are selectively chosen to illustrate exclusionary practices without a complete universe of municipal land-use petitions.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Spatial boundaries, sewer line locations (Piedmont Triad Council of Governments), bypass alignments (NCDOT), and demographic indicators (2000 Census) draw on objective public records, but GIS processing methods are undocumented—including an apparent misdescription of 'block-level race data' as extracted from Census 2000 Summary File 3 ([PDF Page 10]), unstated neighborhood polygon definitions, and an undocumented calculation that 87% of lost bypass property lies in African American and low-income areas ([PDF Page 15])—while septic failure relies on secondary/anecdotal reports.
confounding: High concern: The empirical analysis relies on descriptive spatial overlays and narrative episodes without statistical or engineering adjustment for potential confounders such as topography, soil percolation, lot density, distance to trunk lines, developer-installed infrastructure financing, or municipal capital cost differentials (e.g., the cited $720,000 estimate for a lift station and force main in White Level vs. $268,000 on South Third Street, [PDF Pages 12-13]), although stark adjacent disparities (West End contiguous to the sewer treatment plant; White Level across from Club at Mill Creek) provide strong contextual evidence.
attrition: Can't tell / substantial missingness for household sanitation condition: Cross-sectional Census and municipal GIS boundary/sewer layers have full administrative coverage (aside from unexplained 'no data' polygons in Figures 2-4), but household-level septic failure data suffer from severe non-participation because African American homeowners were reluctant to allow a systematic survey of septic system function out of fear of property condemnation ([PDF Page 13]).
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: The article contains no standalone Methods section, pre-specified protocol, or systematic inventory of all council annexation, rezoning, and utility decisions; qualitative 'participant observation' and 'content analysis of town council deliberations' ([PDF Page 1]) are asserted without reporting sampling frames, coding rules, or systematic treatment of counter-examples.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate spatial and documentary grounding with weak coding transparency: Municipal legal mechanisms—corporate boundaries, Extraterritorial Jurisdiction (ETJ), satellite annexation, industrial rezonings (R-20 to M1, M-2), and Water Quality Critical Area (WQCA / Balance of Watershed) overlays—are accurately described, mapped from public GIS files, and linked to dated Mebane City Council minutes (1991-2002), but statutory citations rely on secondary summaries and no systematic coding protocol across all municipal zoning/annexation actions is presented ([PDF Pages 7-10]).
outcome_measurement_quality: Mixed (strong spatial network presence, weak primary sanitation/health measurement): Municipal sewer access is directly measured via geo-coded sewer line maps overlaid on neighborhood boundaries and Census racial composition ([PDF Pages 10-11], Figure 3), whereas septic tank failure and microbial water contamination are not measured through systematic primary data collection by the authors, relying instead on qualitative reports and a brief summary of a secondary 2002 EPA surface-water study (rounds of 7, 5, and 5 samples) ([PDF Pages 11-13]).
where_found: Methodological overview in INTRODUCTION ([PDF Page 1]) and CONCLUSIONS ([PDF Page 16]); demographic and spatial data sources in THE CASE STUDY CONTEXT ([PDF Pages 4-6], Figures 1-2), Denial of Sewer Service ([PDF Pages 10-13], Figure 3), and Highway Re-Routing ([PDF Pages 13-15], Figure 4); qualitative municipal documentary evidence in DISCRIMINATORY TACTICS ([PDF Pages 7-15]), NOTE 1 ([PDF Page 17]), and REFERENCES ([PDF Pages 17-19]). No standalone Methods section is present.

study_design_identified: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (121 village clusters comprising 328 analyzed rural villages randomized into 50 treatment clusters and 71 control clusters across four provinces in the Democratic Republic of Congo)
why_tool_chosen: The Methods section establishes that the study is a prospective cluster-randomized controlled trial in which multi-village geographic clusters (121 clusters containing 328 analyzed villages) were randomly allocated to receive the community-level VEA WASH and governance intervention (50 clusters) or serve as controls (71 clusters), directly matching the RoB 2 cluster-randomized trials variant.
overall_rating: High
selection_bias: Some concerns — While all 121 village clusters were randomized simultaneously using Stata V.16 prior to intervention delivery, individual households (4 per village) were identified and recruited post-randomization at endline via a random-walk protocol without a baseline household roster or reported household non-response/replacement tracking.
measurement_bias: High risk — All primary and secondary outcomes were self-reported by unblinded household respondents and village leaders following a participatory behaviour-change and 'Healthy Village' certification intervention; additionally, one questionnaire module covered programme participation (potentially unmasking initially blinded enumerators), and no independent physical spot-checks or water-quality assays were reported.
confounding: Low risk — Computer-generated cluster randomization stratified by province and number of villages per cluster achieved strong balance across observable time-invariant household and respondent characteristics (Table 1, all p >= 0.153), and intention-to-treat regressions controlled for randomization strata.
attrition: Low risk — All 121 randomized clusters (50 treatment clusters containing 145 villages and 71 control clusters containing 183 villages) were retained at endline, with complete primary outcome data reported for all 1,312 sampled households (4 per village), although household refusal or replacement rates during the endline random walk are not reported.
reporting_bias: Some concerns — The trial was registered on the AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0004648) and reports all four preregistered primary outcomes and five preregistered subgroup analyses, but the authors explicitly disclose a post-hoc split of the secondary health behaviour and knowledge domain into three separate outcomes after inspecting the data, alongside minor shifts in how village water-point counts were operationalized as an index in Table 3.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — Assignment to the DRC government's national Villages et Ecoles Assainis (VEA) administrative programme is cleanly defined at the cluster level, and the paper clearly documents the 7 official 'Healthy Village' certification norms and 9-step Health Zone/community institutional protocol (signed Health Zone agreement, elected WASH committee, Chief Medical Officer certification), though local water governance outcomes are measured via village-leader self-report rather than administrative audits.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak to moderate — Primary water and sanitation infrastructure outcomes use standard WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) definitions and multi-item secondary constructs use standardized summary indices, but every outcome (facility type, collection time/volume, hygiene/sanitation behaviours, water governance, and 2-week child morbidity) relies exclusively on single-wave endline self-report at a median of 5 months post-intervention without structured direct observation or objective testing.

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative multi-tier case study using Problem-Driven Governance and Political Economy (PGPE) analysis (81 semi-structured interviews and group discussions across national, regional, district, ward, and village levels, plus policy and grey-literature review)
why_tool_chosen: The study's empirical design (Section 2, PDF pp. 4-6) is a primary qualitative field case study based on 81 semi-structured interviews and group discussions across four administrative tiers in 6 purposively sampled Tanzanian districts, supplemented by policy/document review. There is no quantitative experimental/quasi-experimental comparator or statistical analysis (brief descriptive budget figures and a non-representative field check of baseline forms serve only to contextualize qualitative implementation findings), making the CASP Qualitative Checklist the matching tool under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 No and 2 Can't tell items out of Q1-Q9)
selection_bias: Moderate concern — Purposive district sampling intentionally spanned performance tiers (6 of 42 NSC districts combining initially outstanding, regular, and low performance) and included 81 interviews/group discussions across national, regional, district, ward, and village levels (PDF p. 5, Section 2.2), but criteria for choosing the 3 regions, 9 wards, 15 villages, and 'random villagers' who attended triggering are unreported, and districts themselves avoided very isolated or culturally challenging communities in Year 1 (PDF p. 9, Section 4.1).
measurement_bias: Moderate concern — Interviews were conducted mostly in Swahili using handwritten notes compared within the team prior to transcription rather than audio recordings, no semi-structured interview guide is provided, and researcher/NGO positionality is not examined (PDF p. 6, Section 2.2; p. 14, Acknowledgments). In addition, the authors document high error rates in routine village-collected NSC baseline questionnaires (40% significantly wrong in their non-representative field check; PDF p. 11, Section 4.3).
confounding: Not applicable as a causal-inference estimator (non-comparative qualitative political-economy case study) — The study does not estimate quantitative causal treatment effects, though it explicitly maps contextual and institutional factors (historical Ujamaa campaigns, fiscal centralization, delayed transfers, per diem incentives, and weak village solidarity networks) shaping implementation (PDF pp. 4-8, Sections 2.1 and 3.1-3.3).
attrition: Low concern / largely not applicable — Cross-sectional qualitative fieldwork with high participation: all approached respondents except one agreed to participate across 81 completed interviews and group discussions (PDF p. 6, Section 2.2), and there was no longitudinal follow-up cohort.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern — Results systematically report across all five pre-specified project management functions (Planning, Budgeting, Coordination, Implementation, Monitoring; Tables 1-2, PDF pp. 5, 9-12), including unfavorable findings, but absence of transparent coding rules, district-by-district disaggregation (e.g., comparing high- vs low-performing sampled districts), and verbatim participant quotations limits auditability against selective narrative synthesis.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — Clearly identifies and distinguishes relevant Tanzanian policy and administrative governance instruments (1998 Policy Paper on Local Government Reform, 2010 inter-ministerial MoU, 2011 Draft Sanitation and Hygiene Policy, 2012 NSC Concept Note, intergovernmental transfer rules including the unimplemented 20% district-to-village revenue share, and public-sector per diem rules), separating de jure mandates from de facto local bureaucratic practice, though relying on policy/grey documents without granular statutory citations (PDF pp. 6-10, Sections 3.1-3.2 and 4.1-4.2).

study_design_identified: Legal-historical and institutional policy case study (doctrinal-empirical synthesis of UK electricity and water privatisation, statutory/regulatory reforms, judicial review, and secondary administrative statistics across two sector case studies)
why_tool_chosen: The paper collects no primary qualitative interview/ethnographic data (ruling out CASP and MMAT), implements no systematic literature search or screening protocol (ruling out AMSTAR 2), and conducts no primary survey, cohort, experimental, or quasi-experimental econometric analysis with a comparator arm (ruling out RoB 2, ROBINS-I, and JBI checklists). Instead, written by a legal scholar, it combines doctrinal analysis of British utility statutes, regulatory licences, and High Court judicial review with two institutional/legal-historical case studies ('paying for water' and 'fuel poverty') drawing on secondary official and NGO statistics, matching the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework in RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Strong legal-doctrinal accuracy and institutional contextualization, but weak empirical causal identification, sampling, and measurement transparency
selection_bias: High concern: the two sector case studies (paying for water and fuel poverty) and supporting secondary reports are selected purposively to illustrate an interpretivist argument without transparent inclusion/exclusion criteria, and no comparative analysis is conducted against non-privatised UK jurisdictions (such as Scottish water) despite acknowledging their distinct legal arrangements.

attrition: Not applicable (institutional and legal-historical case study synthesizing statutes, case law, and aggregate secondary administrative reports rather than tracking an empirical participant cohort).
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: there is no pre-specified research protocol or systematic evidence selection framework, and quantitative data points (such as selected baseline/peak disconnection years) are cited narratively without comprehensive tabular reporting across the 1990–2006 period.
legal_measurement_quality: Strong: primary UK statutes (Water Act 1989, Electricity Act 1989 s. 3A as amended, Water Industry Act 1999, Utilities Act 2000, Water Act 2003), regulatory licence enforcement structures, Vulnerable Groups Regulations, and the High Court judicial review ruling in R v Director General of Water Services ex parte Oldham Borough Council (1998) are accurately specified with explicit territorial boundaries across England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland.

study_design_identified: Repeated cross-sectional observational municipal-level regression study (Coulter distributional inequity index calculation and separate cross-sectional Tobit and OLS regressions for 152 South Korean local governments in 2010, 2016, and 2021)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study is a quantitative observational study analyzing secondary administrative records for 152 municipal water utilities in three separate cross-sections (2010, 2016, and 2021) via cross-sectional Tobit and OLS regressions examining political, regional, fiscal, and operational correlates of distributional inequity scores. Because no specific intervention or policy change is evaluated with a quasi-experimental or comparative longitudinal counterfactual design (ruling out ROBINS-I) and no incident cohort follow-up of initially outcome-free units is conducted (ruling out JBI Cohort), the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching instrument.
overall_rating: High concern
selection_bias: Low concern within the defined municipal target universe: The study includes all 152 city and county (si/gun) local water supply operators out of 161 nationwide after explicitly excluding 9 special/metropolitan cities and special self-governing provinces. Excluding metropolitan utilities is substantively reasonable given structural scale differences, though it limits generalizability to Korea's largest urban water systems.
measurement_bias: High concern: Although underlying water utility inputs come from official Ministry of Environment Water Supply Statistics, applying Coulter's extensive population-share allocation formula (Xi/S - Ei) to intensive rate and unit-price variables (average unit price, cost recovery rate, revenue water ratio, and water supply rate) severely distorts municipal inequity measurement by making scores largely a mechanical function of population share Ei (as partially acknowledged in Footnote 14). Additionally, customer satisfaction is proxied solely by raw complaint counts, penalizing municipalities with lower-than-expected per-capita complaints as inequitable.
confounding: High concern: While regressions control for binary private consignment and local public enterprise status alongside administrative unit (si/gun), financial independence, and per-capita local tax burden, critical confounders are omitted—most notably municipal population size/density (which mechanically enters the Coulter benchmark Ei and correlates strongly with si/gun status and fiscal independence), mountainous terrain, water source proximity, resident income, and unobserved time-invariant municipal heterogeneity across the three waves.
attrition: Low concern: Administrative data cover a complete balanced sample of all 152 target municipal local governments (si and gun) in each of the three analyzed cross-sections (2010, 2016, and 2021; Obs = 152 across Tables 5 and 8-15) with no missing observations.
reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported (No information). Full regression tables for all six dependent variables across all three years (Tables 9-14) and OLS robustness checks (Appendix Table 15) are reported, and the author candidly notes limitations regarding Coulter unit-price interpretation (Footnote 14) and Tobit non-censoring (Section 4.2). However, municipality-level adjustment tables omit five indicators and part of the sample due to space limits (Footnote 12), several municipalities are anonymized, Table 3 contains formula/translation errors, Table 5 has a population SD typo (250,34), and Tables 12 and 13 display identical LR chi-square, Pseudo R2, and Log likelihood values across all three years.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate for basic administrative classification, weak for institutional depth: Statutory/administrative categories—si vs gun administrative status, local public enterprise special-account status (Local Public Enterprises Act special account vs general account), private operational consignment to K-water, fiscal independence ratio, and per-capita local tax burden—are accurately sourced from official government portals (MOIS, NEC, NSO, ME), but coded only as coarse binary or aggregate variables without municipal tariff ordinance structures, block rates, or consignment contract duration/targets.
outcome_measurement_quality: High concern (weak construct validity of composite outcome despite reliable raw administrative data): Raw municipal indicators (average unit price, cost recovery rate, revenue water ratio, water supply coverage rate, staff count, and complaint count) are drawn from standardized national Water Supply Statistics (ME, 2023), but transforming intensive prices and percentages through Coulter's population-share index yields implausible equity benchmarks (e.g., a theoretical unit price of 5,734 won/m3 for a populous city in Section 4.1) and conflates low complaint volume with distributional inequity.

overall_rating: Moderate concern (5 Can't tell / 0 No items)

study_design_identified: Retrospective cohort / life-course event-history survival study (semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards and Kaplan-Meier analysis of longitudinal residential and water-access trajectories reconstructed from a nationally representative 2000 retrospective survey)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies
why_tool_chosen: Although data were gathered in a single-wave 2000 retrospective life-history survey (EMIUB), the empirical design reconstructs longitudinal person-time cohorts starting from an outcome-free state at age 15 (or city arrival after age 15) up to event occurrence or right-censoring, analyzed via Kaplan-Meier survivor curves and time-varying Cox proportional hazards models. There is no discrete policy/intervention evaluation with a comparator arm (ruling out ROBINS-I), making the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies the best-fitting instrument to evaluate baseline outcome-free status, person-time follow-up, censoring/loss to follow-up, time-varying confounding, and survival modeling.
overall_rating: Some concern
selection_bias: Some concern: Uses a nationally representative two-stage stratified probability sample (EMIUB 2000) with sampling weights and includes 294 former Ouagadougou residents interviewed elsewhere in Burkina Faso, but retrospective sampling of living residents in 2000 excludes deceased persons and international emigrants (survivor/emigrant selection bias) and omits survey response rates.
measurement_bias: Some concern: Multi-decade life-course exposures and water transitions (from age 6/15 up to age 64) rely on retrospective self-report in a low-literacy setting; an AGEVEN age-event calendar mitigated temporal ordering errors, but recall lapse over decades and projection-based imputation of urban/rural status at age 6 introduce potential misclassification.
confounding: Some concern: Time-varying Cox proportional hazards models adjust for historical decade, sex, education, economic activity, marital status, childhood residence at age 6, housing tenure, urban zoning, and tenure-by-zone interactions, but direct time-varying household income/wealth, connection fees/tariffs, household size, and polygamous compound headship are unmeasured.
attrition: Some concern: Although prospective wave-to-wave attrition does not occur because life histories were collected retrospectively in 2000, unobserved selection/loss from pre-2000 mortality and international emigration could not be measured or adjusted for, while right-censoring for internal out-migration from Ouagadougou (424 in first-access; 310 in first-loss) relies on an untested non-informative censoring assumption and survey non-response rates are unreported.
reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-registered protocol or analysis plan is mentioned; regression tables omit confidence intervals/standard errors and proportional-hazards assumption diagnostics, highlight marginal p < 0.15 effects, and contain an unexplained minor discrepancy in the first-loss sample size between Table 1 (1,226 persons at risk) and text on PDF page 12 (1,220 people).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / coarse proxy quality: Formal municipal allotment/zoning status (which legally governs eligibility for ONEA piped connections) and property tenure are operationalized via respondent-reported residence in three broad spatial zones (downtown, zoned periphery, non-zoned periphery) and four tenure categories (owner/co-owner, renter, parent's residence, other's residence), without verification of formal titles, exact neighbourhood rezoning/allotment dates, or ONEA connection regulations.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Piped water access (at least one private or shared tap in the dwelling, plot, or yard) and transition dates are systematically tracked across all residence spells lasting >=3 months, distinguishing residential moves from in-situ connections/disconnections, but rely on unverified retrospective recall, conflate exclusive household taps with shared or potentially locked compound taps, and omit service continuity or water quality.
where_found: Study design, sampling, retrospective recall/survivor-bias discussion, Cox hazard specification, risk-set definitions, and covariates are detailed in 'Data and Methods' (PDF pp. 5-8, Table 1, and Notes 1-7 on PDF p. 17). Empirical survival curves, multivariable hazard ratios, and tenure-by-zone interactions are reported in 'Results' (PDF pp. 8-15, Figures 1-3, Tables 2-7), with institutional context on ONEA and land zoning in 'Water Access in Ouagadougou' (PDF pp. 4-5) and 'Discussion and Conclusion' (PDF pp. 15-17).

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative historical-geographical case study combining archival/policy document analysis and stakeholder/vendor interviews in Kampala (Kisenyi I and II parishes)
why_tool_chosen: Although the main body reads as a historical-geographical narrative without a standalone Methods section, Endnote 61 and interview citations (Notes 48, 54, 63, 67, 68, 71, 72, 74, 78) establish that the study rests on primary qualitative fieldwork conducted in Kisenyi I and II in 2006 and 2008 (interviews with 30 standpost water vendors, NWSC/Kampala Water officials, consultants, community leaders, caretakers, and NGO staff) alongside archival colonial and policy documents. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, a primary qualitative documentary and interview-based field case study maps directly to the CASP Qualitative Checklist (whereas the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is reserved for studies fitting none of the six conventional empirical designs).
overall_rating: High methodological concern (4 Can't tell items and 2 No items across Q1-Q9)
selection_bias: High concern / Can't tell: Primary fieldwork was confined to Kisenyi I and II parishes (Endnote 61, PDF p. 16) without justification of site selection across Kampala's informal settlements; recruitment procedures for the 30 standpost vendors and institutional informants are unreported, utility offices assisted the research (Acknowledgements, PDF p. 15), and ordinary low-income tenants/non-users are not documented as direct interviewees.

confounding: High concern (descriptive qualitative design without counterfactual control): Temporal changes in Kampala water coverage, new connections after the 2004 connection policy, and lower water prices under the Kisenyi pre-paid pilot co-occurred with donor subsidies, internal management restructuring, population growth, and political standpost campaigns without design or analytical controls.
attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable: Although interviews were conducted in two waves (2006 and 2008, Endnote 61, PDF p. 16), the study is not structured as a longitudinal panel and provides no information on informant follow-up or systematic tracking of installed pre-paid standposts over time.
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Absence of an explicit qualitative coding protocol, lack of verbatim interviewee quotes, and unattributed empirical claims on PDF pp. 12-13 (pp. 50-51) regarding loss of vendor credit and landlord coercion introduce risk of selective narrative synthesis, though both strengths and drawbacks of utility reforms are discussed.

study_design_identified: Concurrent mixed-methods study ('partially mixed concurrent equal status design') combining an analytical cross-sectional household questionnaire survey (n = 317/318 analyzed from 360 surveyed) with qualitative focus group discussions (12 FGDs), observations, and transect walks across four community-managed urban water schemes
why_tool_chosen: Chapter 3 (Section 3.1, PDF pp. 67-69) explicitly designs and executes a primary empirical mixed-methods study ('partially mixed concurrent equal status design') integrating a quantitative household survey strand (RQ1-RQ2, analyzed via logistic regression and Chi-square tests) with a qualitative strand of 12 focus group discussions, observations, and transect walks (RQ3, analyzed via Constant Comparison Analysis). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, genuine mixed-methods primary studies combining qualitative and quantitative empirical components must be appraised with the MMAT (using Quantitative non-randomized items 3.1-3.5 for the analytical cross-sectional exposure-outcome survey component alongside Screening S1-S2, Qualitative 1.1-1.5, and Mixed-Methods 5.1-5.5).
overall_rating: High methodological concern (limited by weakest quantitative non-randomized component; qualitative substantiation and mixed-methods integration items rated Can't tell due to truncation after PDF p. 101; no numeric score per MMAT 2018)
selection_bias: High concern: The four studied schemes (Wandiege, Obunga, Asengo, Paga) were purposively selected from seven SANA schemes in collaboration with SANA's director and scheme management teams specifically to contrast two high-performing, one average, and one poorly performing scheme (Section 3.5, PDF pp. 83-85). Within settlements, households were drawn from the 2012 Kenya Independent Voter Register (potentially excluding unregistered informal-settlement residents), located with local chiefs and SANA staff, and restricted to interviewing the eldest household member during 8:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m. field hours (PDF pp. 70-72), yielding a 59%-84% female sample (Table 4.1, PDF p. 92), with replacement of unlocated households. FGD participants were purposively sampled and interviewed at community water offices (PDF pp. 75-76).
measurement_bias: High concern: Exposure (community participation) and outcome variables are unvalidated single-item self-report binary survey items administered face-to-face after community entry facilitated by local chiefs and SANA staff (PDF pp. 72-75, 94-100), creating strong social desirability and courtesy bias. Crucially, RQ1 analyzes all n = 317 respondents on satisfaction with the committee managing their 'main source of water' even though ~19% of respondents primarily relied on non-scheme sources (wells, boreholes, springs, rivers, private vendors; Table 4.2, PDF p. 94), misclassifying exposure and outcome, and regresses satisfaction on contemporaneous attitudinal willingness items (WILLTOPAY, CONTRIBUTION, INTERVENE).
confounding: High concern: In the accessible RQ1 multivariate logistic regression (Section 4.3.2, PDF pp. 99-100), binary committee satisfaction is regressed solely on seven participatory indicators with zero adjustment for household socioeconomic status, gender, education, primary water source, or scheme fixed effects—despite large cross-scheme differences in demographics and satisfaction (81.0% in Wandiege vs. 16.5% in Paga; Tables 4.1-4.3) that severely confound pooled household associations. RQ2 similarly relies on unadjusted Chi-square tests (Table 3.1, PDF p. 69) and logistic models in truncated Chapter 5 with no confounder control strategy specified in Methods (Section 3.2.2, PDF p. 75).
attrition: Some concern / Can't tell: Cross-sectional design without longitudinal follow-up, but sample denominators are inconsistently reported without reconciliation across chapters (400 voters randomly drawn at 100 per locality [PDF p. 70], non-located households replaced [PDF p. 71], 360 households surveyed at a reported 86% response rate [PDF p. 71], N = 318 stated in Table 3.1 and Section 3.2.2 [PDF pp. 69, 74], and n = 317 analyzed in Tables 4.1-4.6 [PDF pp. 92-101]; similarly, FGD totals are reported as n = 91 in Table 3.1 [PDF p. 69] versus 71 across subgroups in Table 3.4 [PDF p. 78]).
reporting_bias: Can't tell (some concern): No study protocol or pre-analysis plan is mentioned (typical for a 2015 dissertation), internal sample counts vary without explanation across tables (360 vs. 318 vs. 317 survey; 91 vs. 71 FGD), and PDF pages 102-215 (Section 4.4, Chapters 5-7, and Appendices including the 57-item survey questionnaire in Appendix C) were truncated in the provided source text, preventing verification of whether all planned items and analyses were completely reported.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / indirect operationalization (partially unassessable for Chapter 6): Chapter 1 descriptively outlines informal tenure characteristics (PDF p. 17), Kenya's Water Reform Act of 2002 and KIWASCO's Delegated Management Model in Obunga (Section 1.3.2, PDF pp. 33-34), and community-elected self-help/trustee structures across the four schemes (Sections 1.3.1-1.3.4, PDF pp. 32-38), while the Table of Contents lists Section 6.2.5 ('Extent of Institutional Formalization', truncated after PDF p. 101). However, the quantitative models do not measure legal or institutional governance rules directly, relying instead on self-reported household participation and willingness items (Table 4.4, PDF p. 97).

selection_bias: High risk of selection bias: at the settlement level, partner NGOs selectively entered slums where residents could afford cost-recovery payments while passing over destitute settlements (PDF p. 12), and one partner's area (BAWPA) was excluded from the survey for security reasons (PDF pp. 3-4). measurement_bias: Moderate risk of measurement bias: water source, defecation practice, hygiene lesson recall/compliance, committee participation, and poverty-tier criteria rely on unblinded household questionnaire self-reports (primarily female respondents, PDF p. 3) without microbiological water testing, metered volume tracking, or structured behavioural observation. confounding: High risk of confounding: the quantitative impact evaluation relies on a post-only comparison of 491 beneficiary and 639 non-beneficiary households with no pre-intervention baseline and no multivariable regression or statistical adjustment. attrition: Can't tell / unclear risk of missing data: as a single post-intervention cross-sectional survey, longitudinal panel attrition does not apply, although qualitative accounts note poor residents dropping out of committees and defaulting on monthly water bills (PDF pp. 7, 11). reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: no study protocol or pre-analysis plan is referenced, and the published paper is a secondary condensation of a 2001 external consultancy report 'summarized by Stephen Mezulianik and Vicky Blagbrough', the latter serving as WaterAid's Programme Learning Facilitator (PDF p. 1). outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: survey outcomes clearly disaggregate drinking water source types and inside- vs. outside-slum location (Table 2) as well as sanitary vs. high-risk defecation facilities (Table 3), complemented by rich qualitative accounts of tariff structures, loan repayment schedules, and committee governance (PDF pp. 5-12). study_design_identified: Two sequential randomized field experiments: (1) a parallel compound-randomized controlled trial of face-to-face tenant outreach/engagement (N = 2,584 compounds with tenants across 6 settlements) and (2) a two-stage street-level cluster-randomized controlled trial of utility service-contract enforcement via credible disconnection notices (147 street clusters across 4 settlements; 327 treated eligible compounds, 322 within-cluster spillover controls, and 674 pure-cluster eligible controls).
why_tool_chosen: Selected RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant) because the study is a primary experimental evaluation whose focal legal/institutional intervention—contract enforcement of utility disconnection clauses, which is also the sole experiment followed up for water/sanitation access, welfare, and rental market outcomes—was randomized at the street-cluster level (147 street clusters in a two-stage cluster-randomized design, Section 5-6) across multi-household compounds. The cluster-RCT variant captures all standard parallel-trial RoB 2 domains (applicable to both the engagement and enforcement experiments) while additionally assessing D1b (timing of identification/recruitment of individual tenants within compounds/clusters), which directly applies to the endline tenant survey.
overall_rating: Some concerns
selection_bias: Low risk for compound-level administrative outcomes (eligible accounts were enumerated from the utility database and August 2018 phone census prior to random assignment). Some concerns for endline tenant-level survey outcomes because one tenant per compound was randomly sampled 9 months post-intervention, after the enforcement treatment significantly increased the proportion of compounds renting out dwellings by 13.5 percentage points (from 58.9% to 72.4%, p<0.001), potentially altering the composition of surveyed tenants; additionally, two dense multi-story settlements were excluded from the enforcement trial for technical feasibility reasons (external validity limitation).
measurement_bias: Low risk for primary revenue collection and loan repayment outcomes (measured objectively via the automated Jisomee Mita electronic utility billing platform) and for enumerator-verified compound connections and physical water meter readings. Some concerns for secondary survey outcomes at 9 months (self-reported monthly water expenditure, weekly water-fetching minutes, perceptions of utility fairness and quality, owner-tenant relationships, and rental income), as participants were unblinded to disconnection notices and survey enumerator blinding within treatment clusters is not reported.
confounding: Low risk. Both interventions used randomized assignment stratified by informal settlement (individual compound randomization for engagement; two-stage street-cluster randomization for contract enforcement). Multi-year pre-intervention administrative payment trajectories (2014 to October 2018, Figure 5) and 45 baseline balance tests (Table A3) confirm strong comparability across arms, and robustness regressions controlling for minor baseline imbalances (water connection status and presence of paying tenants, p<0.05) left treatment estimates unchanged.
attrition: Low risk for primary administrative payment outcomes (0% missing data across all 2,584 compounds in the engagement trial and all 1,001 compounds in the enforcement ITT analysis via automated utility billing records). Some concerns for secondary 9-month follow-up survey outcomes in enforcement-treatment clusters (out of 649 eligible compounds: N=589-608 for compound water/sanitation indicators, N=474 [27% missing] for physical meter readings, N=334 [49% missing] for household monthly water expenditure, and N=357-403 for tenant survey outcomes), with no arm-specific survey attrition balance tests reported.
reporting_bias: Some concerns. The experiments were registered in the AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0003556), primary payment analyses follow the specified ITT equations, and all individual sub-indicators underlying the Anderson (2008) summary indices are fully reported in Appendix Tables A1, A2, and A6. However, maternal-reported under-five child health outcomes were collected at endline and omitted from analysis post hoc (explicitly disclosed in Section 8.5), and the follow-up survey analyses (Tables 7-8) restrict the control group to within-cluster control compounds in enforcement-treatment clusters rather than the pure control clusters specified in Equation (2).
legal_measurement_quality: Strong. The contractual enforcement exposure is grounded in written utility upgrade contracts signed by property owners and Kenya's 2016 Water Act / WASREB regulatory framework, and is operationalized via explicit administrative arrears rules (>US$ 25 consumption balance plus missed monthly payments), standardized tablet scripts and posted 14-day disconnection notices with hardship appeal channels (Appendix B), and exact administrative tracking of notice delivery (299/327 = 91.4%), physical disconnections (96 compounds), and reconnections.
outcome_measurement_quality: Strong for utility financial outcomes (5 years of high-frequency electronic billing, invoice, consumption, and loan-repayment records) and adequate-to-strong for household water and sanitation outcomes, which combine direct enumerator observation of piped water and pour-flush sewer connections and on-site meter readings with noisy self-reported water expenditure and weekly fetching time (with no microbiological water quality testing and unanalyzed child health data).

overall_rating: Serious
selection_bias: Low risk: Near-census coverage of all Minas Gerais municipalities served solely by Copasa-MG/Copanor (572 of 581 municipalities), with transparent, non-outcome-driven exclusion of 9 municipalities served by additional water utilities whose unmeasured customers would distort the municipal CadÚnico denominator.

attrition: Low risk: Balanced administrative panel of 572 of 581 Copasa-MG municipalities in 2020-2021 (9 multi-provider municipalities excluded by pre-specified structural rule) and 570 municipalities in the 2018-2021 robustness check (only 2 municipalities missing 2018 DIST data, <0.4% attrition).
reporting_bias: No information: No pre-analysis plan or pre-registered study protocol is reported; however, results are reported consistently across non-parametric Wilcoxon tests, three covariate specifications avoiding multicollinearity, and a 2018-2021 panel robustness check.

study_design_identified: Quasi-experimental matched-cohort longitudinal household survey (genetic matching of 8 continuous water supply pilot wards to 8 intermittent water supply control wards using pre-intervention 2006 survey data, followed by 4 post-intervention survey rounds of 3,922 households over 15 months with multivariable OLS regressions) combined with a household- and utility-level net present value (NPV) cost-benefit analysis.
why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates a non-randomized municipal infrastructure and tariff reform intervention (conversion from intermittent to continuous 24x7 piped water supply with universal metering, increasing block tariffs, and removal of free public taps/borewells) against a matched comparator arm (eight intermittent supply wards selected via genetic matching) using longitudinal panel surveys and econometric regression. ROBINS-I is the exact dedicated instrument for non-randomized comparative studies of policy/infrastructure interventions.
overall_rating: Serious
selection_bias: Moderate risk — Households were enrolled in November 2010–February 2012, roughly 2–4 years after the 2008 CWS pilot rollout rather than at intervention inception, using systematic landmark-walk sampling restricted to households with a child under age 5 (n = 1,969 CWS; n = 1,953 IWS), without reporting refusal/non-response rates across arms or testing for post-2008 residential mobility.
measurement_bias: Serious risk — Enumerators and respondents could not be blinded to neighborhood CWS versus IWS status; monthly waiting/collection time relied on subjective recall despite respondents multitasking on household chores while waiting; and water bill and volumetric consumption measurement differed systematically across arms because CWS connections were universally metered whereas many IWS and low-SES/tenant households lacked meters or utility bills (and informal side payments in IWS zones were excluded).
confounding: Moderate risk — Eight CWS demonstration wards were non-randomly selected for ease of hydraulic isolation and household-level pre-2008 baseline outcomes were unavailable, but the authors mitigated observable confounding via ward-level genetic matching on a pre-intervention 2006 survey of 15,000 households (matching on SES, household tap/latrine access, garbage collection, pre-CWS delivery frequency, and health spending) combined with household-level SES covariate regressions.
attrition: Serious risk — Out of 3,922 enrolled households (1,969 CWS and 1,953 IWS), Round 2 regression models excluded 30.2% of observations for ongoing expenditures (n = 2,739), 31.5% for total monetary costs (n = 2,688), 21.5% for time spent (n = 3,078), and 12.0% for amortized investment (n = 3,453), while billed-volume analyses suffered severe differential missingness across IWS versus CWS zones and lower wealth quintiles due to unmetered connections and unavailable utility bills, without missing-data adjustment or a round-by-round attrition flow table.
reporting_bias: Moderate risk — No pre-registered protocol or economic pre-analysis plan is cited; Section 4 regressions report Round 2 out of 4 survey rounds (whereas Section 5 NPV equations average across rounds) and collected medical expenses and illness-care time were omitted due to small/undetectable differences, although extensive sensitivity checks across covariates, five utility cost assumptions, and wage-time valuations are transparently reported.
legal_measurement_quality: High — Municipal water service rules, administrative ward boundaries, and tariff reforms under KUWASIP versus status-quo Hubli-Dharwad Municipal Corporation intermittent supply are precisely specified, including universal connection registration, metering charges, flat versus volumetric increasing block tariffs (Rs/kL tiers), decommissioning of free public standpipes and borewells, and World Bank/WSP project finance categories.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate — Durable household infrastructure and storage investments were anchored by physical inspections, a 707-household container measurement subsample, and local retail market price surveys, but primary time-savings and income measures relied on unblinded recall, volumetric consumption relied on partial metered bills differentially missing in IWS and poorer households, and utility-level NPV relied on inconsistent secondary World Bank/WSP cost reports.

selection_bias: High concern: purposive extreme-case selection on the dependent variable ('opposite ends of the SES performance continuum': NYC vs Flint) combined with non-systematic retrieval of secondary, journalistic, and publicly released FOIA documents introduces substantial case- and detail-selection bias, which the authors explicitly acknowledge (PDF pp. 1, 4, 14).
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: polycentricity is operationalized transparently via six structural and functional indicator questions (Table 1) coded independently by both authors to consensus across 24 case-period cells (Table 2), but categorical functional ratings (ADAPTIVE, MIXED, MALADAPTIVE) rely on unblinded retrospective qualitative judgment from secondary and journalistic sources without formal quantitative thresholds (PDF pp. 3-4, 9).
confounding: High risk for causal attribution (though explicitly examined narratively): with N = 2 extreme cases and no counterfactual comparator, process tracing cannot statistically isolate polycentric governance features from major co-occurring structural factors (municipal wealth vs postindustrial fiscal distress, political power asymmetries, systemic racism, and individual executive leadership), although the authors explicitly trace these factors as interacting cross-cutting drivers (PDF pp. 4-6, 10-14).
attrition: Not applicable (retrospective documentary and institutional-historical case study of two municipal water systems across four defined historical periods with complete Table 2 matrix coverage; no human participant cohort subject to follow-up loss).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: no pre-registration or archival search protocol exists and historical narrative construction risks selective emphasis on confirmatory events (explicitly noted by the authors on PDF p. 14), although all six operationalized governance conditions are systematically reported across every case-period in Table 2 and the omission of Carlisle and Gruby's seventh enabling condition is transparently justified in Footnote 1 (PDF pp. 3, 9, 14).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate to strong: accurately distinguishes formal de jure legal structures from de facto enforcement norms across federal, state, and local instruments (U.S. Safe Drinking Water Act, 1989 Surface Water Treatment Rule, Filtration Avoidance Determinations, 1997 NYC Watershed Memorandum of Agreement, Michigan's revised Emergency Manager Law, and the federal Lead and Copper Rule), though legal rules are cited primarily via secondary literature, news journalism, and a USEPA Inspector General report rather than primary statutory/regulatory texts (PDF pp. 2, 7-12).
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate: water system adaptation versus maladaptation is anchored in concrete regulatory, public health, and rate-affordability indicators drawn from official and secondary reports (e.g., EPA FAD renewals, 93% Whole Farm Planning participation, and $464/year average NYC bills vs Flint fecal coliform boil-water advisories, 87 Genesee County Legionnaires' disease cases, elevated water and child blood lead levels, and punitive water rates), though outcomes are synthesized narratively rather than measured uniformly across all four historical periods (PDF pp. 7-8).
where_found: Design, purposive case selection, documentary data sources, independent dual-researcher coding of Table 1 indicators, and causal caveats are reported in Section 3 Methods (PDF p. 4) and Table 1 (PDF p. 3). Historical-institutional narratives and causal pathway diagrams appear in Section 4 and Figures 1-4 (PDF pp. 4-8). Comparative governance ratings appear in Section 5 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 8-12). Cross-cutting confounders and explicit study limitations (selection bias in case details, lack of counterfactuals, generalizability) are discussed in Sections 6-7 (PDF pp. 12-14).

study_design_identified: Qualitative comparative multiple-case study (examining one public, one private, and one community-based water supply scheme in Dar es Salaam using document analysis, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and household interviews)
why_tool_chosen: The Methods section explicitly characterizes the research as a qualitative multiple-case study ('The study was largely qualitative, and deployed a case study methodology', PDF p. 7; 'basically qualitative on the study phenomenon', PDF p. 8) using document analysis, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and household interviews analyzed via contact summaries and thematic/content analysis. Although Table 1 (PDF p. 12, sourced from Kachenje 2017) reports illustrative maximum connection-processing days (30, 3, 6) and actor counts (5, 2, 3) for the three cases, there is no quantitative survey component or statistical analysis, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist (rather than MMAT or JBI Cross-Sectional) the exact matching appraisal tool.
overall_rating: High methodological concern (2 No and 3 Can't tell items)
selection_bias: High concern — Three water supply schemes (one public, one private, one community-based) in Dar es Salaam were purposively selected using unstated selection criteria (PDF p. 7; schemes and neighbourhoods are never named), sample sizes and recruitment methods for key informants, focus groups, and households are completely omitted, and water vending was deliberately excluded despite its acknowledged importance for underserved urban residents (PDF pp. 1, 15).
measurement_bias: High concern — Although four data collection methods (document analysis, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and household interviews) are stated (PDF pp. 1, 2, 7), no interview/FGD guides, recording procedures, field dates, or operationalized coding definitions are reported, and empirical findings rely heavily on unattributed assertions rather than verifiable primary data.
confounding: High concern (not formally applicable to qualitative thematic description, but unaddressed in cross-scheme comparisons) — When comparing administrative responsiveness across the public (30 days), private (3 days), and community-based (6 days) schemes (Table 1, PDF p. 12), differences in scheme scale, customer volume, network complexity, and neighbourhood socioeconomic context are not accounted for.
attrition: Can't tell / No information — Cross-sectional qualitative case study drawing on earlier doctoral fieldwork (Kachenje, 2017); participant refusals, non-response, and incomplete interviews or focus groups are not reported.
reporting_bias: High concern — Substantial selective/incomplete reporting: the Data Analysis section claims that photographs, boxes, summaries, tables, figures, and direct quotations were used to present data from interviews, FGDs, and household interviews (PDF pp. 7-8), yet the published paper contains zero household or FGD data, zero photographs or boxes, only one brief quote from a utility official (PDF p. 14), and a blank Figure 1 diagram on PDF p. 10.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-weak — Key Tanzanian statutes and policies are identified by title and year (Local Government [Urban Authorities] Act No. 7 of 1982, EWURA Act 2001, National Water Policy 2002, NWSDS 2006, Water Resources Management Act No. 11 of 2009, and Water Supply and Sanitation Act 2019; PDF pp. 2, 9-10, 12), and de jure vs. de facto mandate frictions (e.g., DAWASA vs. municipal councils, Wami-Ruvu Basin Water Office abstraction permits vs. service licensing) are coherently mapped. However, specific statutory sections are not cited, Figure 1 (the institutional framework diagram on PDF p. 10) is blank in the published PDF, and empirical fieldwork from 2017 is blended with post-2019 statutory changes without clear temporal separation.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — Water service delivery outcomes are barely measured empirically; the sole concrete service metric is maximum waiting time for new connection processing across the three schemes (30, 3, and 6 days in Table 1, PDF p. 12, cited to Kachenje 2017 without sample size, distribution, or audit source), while household water access, reliability, quality, and tariff affordability are not systematically measured.
where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction (PDF pp. 2-3); Methods — Materials and Methods, Research Design and Process, Sample design, and Data analysis (PDF pp. 7-8); Results and Discussion including Figure 1 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 8-14); Conclusions (PDF pp. 14-15); Ethical considerations and Data availability (PDF p. 17).

study_design_identified: Exploratory convergent mixed-methods primary study (cross-sectional self-administered questionnaire survey N = 97 with open-ended qualitative thematic content analysis n = 30, combined with observational chronometric restroom use duration measurement N = 56) situated within a doctrinal/normative legal analysis
why_tool_chosen: The article conducts a primary empirical mixed-methods investigation combining quantitative components (a structured cross-sectional survey of N = 97 respondents analyzed via EFA, Welch's ANOVA, OLS regression, and mediation, plus chronometric restroom dwell-time observations of N = 56 users) with a qualitative component (thematic content analysis of open-ended narrative responses from n = 30 respondents in Section 3.2 / Table 3), explicitly triangulating both strands to inform its legal-governance argument. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) is the required instrument for genuine mixed-methods primary studies, using Quantitative Descriptive items 4.1-4.5 because the quantitative data describe cross-sectional user perceptions/experiences and observed usage durations without an experimental or quasi-experimental policy/intervention comparator.
overall_rating: High methodological concern (weak empirical quality; constrained by non-representative convenience sampling, low scale reliability and coding contradictions, absence of inferential testing for chronometric observations, and integrative reliance on unreported queuing simulations)
selection_bias: High concern: Both empirical strands use convenience sampling with severe demographic and contextual skew. The survey (N = 97) recruited university students and unspecified social media users, yielding 72.2% women and 63.9% aged 18-29 (pp. 5-6, 14), with no sampling frame or response rate reported. The chronometric study observed N = 56 users during a single 40-minute midday interval at one university building in Gyor (p. 9), limiting generalizability to broader municipal public toilets or tourism settings discussed in the paper (pp. 4, 15).
measurement_bias: High concern: Survey constructs rely on an unvalidated ad hoc questionnaire with sub-threshold internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.601; McDonald's omega = 0.640, p. 6), self-reported recall, and a direct Likert polarity contradiction between Table 2's footnote ('1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree', p. 7) and the main text ('lower scores indicate stronger agreement', pp. 6-7). Chronometric restroom observations (N = 56, pp. 5-6, 9) combine entry-to-exit time without separating internal waiting, fixture use, and handwashing, omit external queue time, lack inter-rater reliability protocols, and display discrepant means between Table 4 (~126 s men, ~159 s women) and the text (121.25 s men, 136.63 s women, p. 9).
confounding: High concern: Gender comparisons on survey items (Welch's ANOVA, Table 2, p. 7) and observational restroom usage times (Section 3.3, p. 9) are completely unadjusted. Multiple linear regressions (N = 90, p. 7) adjust only for binary gender and coarse ordinal age brackets (plus an experience composite), omitting key confounders such as parental/caregiving status, disability or health needs, frequency of public-space travel, facility design, and peak internal queue congestion during time observations.
attrition: Can't tell / Moderate concern for item and survey nonresponse: No longitudinal follow-up applies, but overall survey response rate is unreported, 7 of 97 respondents (7.2%) are excluded from correlation/regression models (N = 90) without explicit missing-data accounting (potentially linked to an unexplained 'Hungarian subsample' restriction on p. 5), and only 30 of 97 respondents (30.9%) provided evaluable open-ended qualitative responses (p. 8).
reporting_bias: High concern: No pre-registration or full survey instrument is provided. Section 3.1 selectively reports statistics only for the four survey items showing significant gender differences (Table 2, pp. 6-7) while omitting estimates for non-significant items; Hypothesis H4 is declared 'clearly support[ed]' using raw means alone with no inferential test (pp. 9-10); and Sections 4.1 and 4.5 repeatedly cite 'queuing simulations' (pp. 10, 15) whose methods, parameters, and results never appear in Methods or Findings.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate doctrinal framing, not empirically operationalized: The article accurately identifies relevant EU/UN equality and sanitation instruments (Council Directive 2004/113/EC, EU Charter Art. 23, UNGA Res. 64/292 & 76/153, UN Special Rapporteur reports) and comparative building standards (Hungarian Gov. Reg. Nr. 280/2024, Singapore COPEH, Australian NCC Table F4D4, UK BS 6465 guidance, German ASR A4.1 and DIN 18040-1:2010-1; pp. 2-4, 10, 12-13), organizing them into a conceptual tripartite accountability matrix (Table 1, p. 4). However, legal standards are not coded or measured as empirical exposure variables in the survey or observational study.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Subjective outcomes (perceived safety, satisfaction, need for additional women's toilets, nappy-changing barriers) rely on single-item or low-reliability composite self-reports with inconsistent coding documentation (pp. 6-8). Objective restroom duration is measured in only one university building during a single 40-minute break (N = 56) without isolating waiting vs. fixture service time and without reporting variance (SD/IQR) or inferential statistical tests (pp. 5-6, 9-10).
where_found: Study design, sampling, and hypotheses H1-H4 in Section 2 Methods (PDF pp. 5-6); quantitative survey sample demographics, reliability, Welch's ANOVAs, OLS regressions, and bootstrap mediation in Section 3.1 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 6-8); qualitative thematic content analysis and verbatim excerpts in Section 3.2 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 8-9); chronometric restroom duration observations in Section 3.3 and Table 4 (PDF pp. 9-10); doctrinal/regulatory framework in Section 1 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 2-5) and integrative legal discussion in Sections 4.1-4.4 (PDF pp. 10-14); methodological limitations in Section 4.5 (PDF pp. 14-15); ethics and consent statements on PDF p. 16.
